Industry observers note that the U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA. The law aims to shorten review timelines for infrastructure projects and protect permits from later revocation, among other provisions. But beyond the technical details, the law has been notable for the unusual coalitions that have arranged in favor and opposed to it: Oil and gas companies, manufacturers, and labor unions are broadly in support, while environmental groups such as the Sierra Club and the Wilderness Society and progressive groups such as the NAACP have lined up against.

What exactly would BAAJA do? Why has the law divided some trade unions against progressives? And can renewable energy outcompete fossil fuels on the free market?

In a recent development, the U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA. The law aims to shorten review timelines for infrastructure projects and protect permits from later revocation, among other provisions. But beyond the technical details, the law has been notable for the unusual coalitions that have arranged in favor and opposed to it: Oil and gas companies, manufacturers, and labor unions are broadly in support, while environmental groups such as the Sierra Club and the Wilderness Society and progressive groups such as the NAACP have lined up against.

What exactly would BAAJA do? Why has the law divided some trade unions against progressives? And can renewable energy outcompete fossil fuels on the free market?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Industry observers note that cameron Abadi: What exactly would BAAJA do? And why is this just such a substantial problem right now in the United States?

Industry observers note that adam Tooze: It’s basically an effort to streamline environmental review, restrict certain legal challenges, make permits—once they are issued—more secure. So, enabling investors to proceed robustly. And it’s aiming basically to enable a more rapid build-out of the electricity transmission system.

It’s such a significant deal because this is a really big problem. Electricity interconnection is a fiendishly difficult technical and legal issue. The Berkeley Lab found that about 2,600 gigawatts of generation and storage projects were seeking grid connection at the end of 2023. And more will have come online since. That’s about twice the existing capacity of the United States’ system. And they spend about five years at least applying for interconnection and entering commercial operation, compared to two years only as recently as a few decades ago. You’ve got projects like a giant wind project in New Mexico, which is supposed to be a transmission line that connects New Mexico to Arizona. It took roughly 17 years from initial development to construction, and the vast majority of that was in the permitting. Pipelines are notorious for exactly the same reasons. So, Mountain Valley Pipeline, which is a gas pipeline 303 miles [long through West Virginia and Virginia], originally billed at $3.5 billion and now finally opened in 2024 at a cost of about $8 billion.

Industry observers note that so there are a fundamental set of issues about not only how American procedures decide whether they are for or against major infrastructure projects but also how long it takes them and how expensive they are. If we had a streamlined process, you could process a bunch of obstructions, do it quickly, make a decision, move on. And instead, we have sort of the worst of both worlds, which is a lack of coherence, political chops, and changes by administrations, which are very pro-renewable energy, for instance, and then very opposed to it—which means that even when you do get the permits, they’re not secure. So it’s a mess.

In a recent development, and this is a mess also against the backdrop of the last effort to break this impasse, which after all was the Biden administration. It’s certainly true now that AI is driving the conversation about the build-out of power supply in the United States. But the conversation started earlier with the push around Bidenomics, which then was instantiated in the form of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. And people like Brian Deese, who was a key architect of green industrial policy under the Biden administration, have stated that, you know, passing the Inflation Reduction Act without permitting reform produced modest results. Passing the Inflation Reduction Act with permitting reform would have made a huge difference. Passing the permitting reform two years before the Inflation Reduction Act had come into effect, setting the stage for the energy and the money that poured through the Inflation Reduction Act, would have been a complete game-changer. In other words, the pace of rollout would have been very dramatic. And I think that, in a sense, is what this conversation currently is about.

And it’s furthermore crucial because it does expose fault lines within the coalitions that you might think of as being supportive to this. So Bidenomics glued a coalition together around the green energy project, around American reindustrialization, but also through extraordinarily complex coalition deals—the “everything bagel” liberalism, patching in a whole variety of different environmental justice groups, activists on behalf of rural America, activists on the behalf of minorities in the United States and underrepresented and discriminated-against communities—and they were all part of the Biden package. [Donald] Trump has blown that up. And what we’re seeing here is also a debate, I think, about what are the terms going to be under which a latest, energized Democratic majority actually attempts to restart the project of green modernization in the United States. That’s why this matters beyond the technicalities.

Industry observers note that CA: We tend to think of the left and unions as a natural coalition. But have there always been tensions between them that run along the fault lines of environmentalism, and is that what’s getting revealed in the debate around this law?

Recent findings suggest that AT: In support of what I think is called BAAJA, you do see an unusually broad coalition of organized labor. It isn’t just building trade unions—sort of, you know, construction-happy pipeline workers or whatever. It is in fact a very broad coalition, including the AFL-CIO. And so, from their point of view, this is clearly an industrial, productivist kind of strategy. And it makes sense, and they’re not wrong. And the estimates are that this would move significant volumes of investment. Not stupendous, not dramatic. If you’ve actually seen the econometrics on this, the numbers are not overwhelming. But they’re real, and every little bit helps. And the obstruction around these problems has been highly significant in a number of individual cases. So the coalition is real.

According to recent reports, but you’re right, there are also blocking oppositionists. In fact, it’s telling that in the Senate vote on the legislation so far the purple state senators—so senators who are exposed to more competitive races—were notably more supportive of this legislation than those in absolutely solid blue Democratic constituencies, where the leverage of other interests really came to the fore. And there are at least two that are very well worth taking seriously that have been articulated.

Sources indicate that one is Bill McKibben, one of the real warhorses of the climate movement in the United States, who mentioned, look, it’s all very well to say that we need an energy transition, so we need more electrical generation capacity and transmission facilities. This is clear. It is true. On the other hand, ultimately what counts here is the level of emissions. And so, more construction, more activity in this realm, is not an unalloyed and unambiguous benefit. And if it’s possible that these changes might in fact open the door to large-scale fossil build-out, then, in fact, this is really an ambiguous a set of proposals. And it’s quite clear that in its bipartisan nature, a little bit like some of the Biden administration legislation as well, they are trying to provide pork and trying to buy support from energy interests across the board.

Industry observers note that and then the other constituency that you might think of as left is represented by a spokesperson like Abigail Dillen of Earthjustice, who is representing what in the American conversation is called an environmental justice point of view, first and foremost. And so, just for clarification’s sake, environmental politics is a very broad church. Climate politics within that comes in different shades as well, but climate politics has this very macroscopic, ultimately global point of view. And one of the answers given by the establishment with regards to climate politics is simply electrify everything, build as much clean energy infrastructure as possible as quickly as possible. But the consequences of that locally can of course be very, very disruptive, not to say incredibly damaging. And this is where the environmental justice movement comes in in the United States, which has a genealogy which really originates in the 1980s and 1990s, centrally concerned with the interests of marginalized communities in the United States, notably Black communities in the American South, who find themselves systematically in harm’s way when it comes to otherwise perhaps interesting and important industrial expansion. And so her argument, and the opposition of environmental justice campaigners around this, is to say, well, it’s all very well that you open the door to this kind of development, but who walks through that door? Which interests are going to take advantage of this, and who is going to lose out?

According to recent reports, and to go back to your big-picture historical question, what you’re seeing there is a confrontation between, if you like, three generations of American radical and progressive politics. One is the classic Latest Deal productivist coalition, which is about a bigger government and facilitating public-private partnerships in various ways that enable large-scale investment and development. And that had very considerable buy-in from trade unions.

Expanding the U.S. grid is vital to staying globally competitive.

It has been revealed that but what we see from the 1960s onward—not necessarily in hostility to organized labor but recognizing the impact of the success of this kind of development and its lopsidedness and its egalitarian tendencies—are the other two constituencies of American progressivism, which are now speaking their voice. These things didn’t emerge at the same time in the 1930s, but you could say in the 1960s we see the development of the ecological movement in the United States, the broad-based opposition to environmental damage, which in many cases has a distinctly upper-middle-class, Sierra Club kind of feel to it.

And then from the late 1970s, 1980s, onward, the environmental justice movement, which is in a sense environmental politics crossed with the Civil Rights Movement in the United States and focusing on environmental concerns. And those three things together come out of the same tradition of American progressivism, you might say, but they are not necessarily on the same page. And their targets are not necessarily the same thing either. And the work that Bidenomics did was to, in some senses, square that circle. And as we’ve noted, that’s the coalition that needs to be rebuilt. And this is a conversation about how that gets done.

According to recent reports, CA: One often hears that renewables now outcompete other sources of energy on economic terms. So why shouldn’t advocates for renewables prefer a law that would presumably create a freer market?

AT: Well, those kind of claims are based on what are so-called comparisons of unsubsidized levelized costs of newly introduced electricity generation. That’s the standard measure. And outfits like Lazard have produced numbers that show, for instance, that onshore wind can be had for a cost of between $37 and $99 per megawatt hour, utility-scale solar for between $40 and $98, combined-cycle natural gas for $51 to $129, and so on and so forth.

And when you make the comparisons on that basis, it’s generally true that solar and onshore wind come out as the optimum strategies. But they’re very, very partial measures of cost. Because what they don’t really account for is intermittency fundamentally. Right now, we really shouldn’t be making comparisons of just pure solar and wind versus gas because gas can be turned on and off once you’ve got the infrastructure. Whereas obviously solar and rain can’t. It depends on the availability of sunshine and wind. So they need to be backed up by batteries. Once you do the backup by batteries, they’re still competitive, but the argument is not as simple as saying that they’re the cheapest.

Sources indicate that but broadly speaking, I, in fact, entirely agree with the general thrust of your message. I’m an optimist on this question. And I think this is also the position, for instance, of the abundance agenda types, [Ezra] Klein and [Derek] Thompson and so on, which is that it’s a totally reasonable argument to make—namely that in the end, these technologies are superior. They are cheaper. People are investing in them. If you look in the pipeline, the pipeline is overwhelmingly renewables. And that’s not for reasons of wokeness. There are issues of intermittency, but the harder we push at this, the more we invest, the more the urgency will be to find solutions to them. And markets that are relatively free, like that of Texas, for instance, have turned out to be huge pioneers of rapid adoption of solar and wind. So I think, broadly speaking, that argument is well merited.

Recent findings suggest that the risk is—and this is where somebody like a McKibben will come in—would be to say, well, that’s all very well, but at the margin, we can’t be certain that this game will play out necessarily in the favor of renewables. And the argument here is not coal anymore. Once upon a time, you might have noted coal could come back as a source of electricity generation. I think that argument is done everywhere outside China, probably. [There are] very few places in the world where coal makes any sense. Nuclear, for those who have environmental concerns about nuclear, [is] also prohibitively expensive. A free market option without subsidy probably kills it completely stone-dead given its costs. The real issue is gas.

It has been revealed that and the lesson here is not abstract—it’s historical. Because in the 2010s, what happened is that the entire calculus of the electricity-generating investment game in the United States was changed by the sudden availability of huge quantities of dirt-cheap shale gas, so fracked gas. And that had the effect of considerably displacing the adoption of wind and solar, which actually progressed more rapidly in Europe because gas prices—despite all of the talk of cheap gas from Russia, it was always nonsense. The really cheap gas comes from Texas, it comes from Pennsylvania, it comes from shale in the United States. And that considerably slowed down the adoption of more sustainable, more renewable energy sources. But broadly speaking, of course, it’s still a win. And folks from within the Obama administration embraced this under the heading of “all of the above” because gas replacing coal is a net win in terms of emissions. You might quibble with this if you think about the methane admitted in the production of gas, but nevertheless, it is a step in the right direction.

It has been revealed that so the general thrust of your question, I think, should be affirmed. You know, we should not be thinking of renewables as a sort of endangered technology that needs protecting against the significant beasts of fossil industry. Are there fossil risks? Yes, but they come largely from innovation in the fossil sector and not the old enemies. Not coal, not nuclear—oil has never really been in the game here anyway for electricity generation, not since the ’70s. But that, to my mind, means that this should be weighed up in terms of exactly how much build-out of which types of energy we expect. It’s not a matter of principle that renewables should favor regulation, fossils should favor deregulation. It’s not as simple as that. It’s a conjunctural specific historical gamble that, in the current moment, the benefits outweigh the downsides.

According to recent reports, what we’re seeing, unfortunately, under Trump is that the biggest build-out and the biggest acceleration of electricity demand in American history—in recent times at least—probably ever in American history actually in terms of sheer volume, is taking place under an administration that seems determined to block renewables and under a permitting system that doesn’t permit a rapid build-out of efficient capacity. And the disaster there is it’s channeling all of that AI demand into gas-fired generation. It’s not epic by global standards; this isn’t China’s coal build-out. But it’s taking America in the wrong direction. And that’s the backdrop also against which this conversation is taking place right now. We see that there is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity or historic opportunity to have accelerated American electrification along green lines, and it’s being obstructed.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi.

According to recent reports, adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze.

Johnson, Tobin reports, could be kicked off the ballot for re-election.

Democratic Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson is fighting to keep his name on the 2027 ballot with his administration is engulfed in a fiscal and leadership meltdown at City Hall.

Election officials are reviewing challenges to more than 25,000 of Johnson's nominating signatures ahead of the Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral election, a threshold fight unfolding just days after his third chief financial officer in 10 months abruptly resigned, Standard & Poor's placed Chicago's credit rating on negative watch and the City Council voted 45-5 to investigate three years of city financial reporting for possible misstatements.

Despite the mounting pressure, Johnson brushed off questions about whether he will survive the ballot challenge.

Recent findings suggest that "Yeah, feeling just fine. I'm going to be on the ballot," Johnson told ABC 7 Chicago about the challenge. "Looking forward to building the safest, most affordable big city in America, and we're going to continue to do that work.".

CHICAGO'S 12-LANGUAGE BALLOTS MAKE ELECTIONS 'HARDER TO MONITOR,' ILLINOIS GOP CHAIR WARNS.

According to recent reports, chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks to demonstrators in Grant Park who were protesting the policies of President Donald Trump and showing their support for union labor on May 1, 2025, in Chicago. (Scott Olson/Getty Images).

Johnson needs 12,500 valid signatures to qualify for Chicago's Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral ballot. Hearing officers at the Chicago Board of Elections are reviewing more than 25,000 signatures challenged by supporters of perennial mayoral candidate Willie Wilson.

Johnson's campaign states 6,718 signatures were not challenged and projects that he would finish with 14,788 valid signatures if the first day's 32% validation rate holds. That would put him 2,288 signatures above the requirement, but the figure is the campaign's estimate, not a final board tally. The objectors say early rulings are favoring their challenge, and the review remains unresolved.

The turmoil inside City Hall accelerated after the sudden departure of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch, who said continuing in the role would "compromise my integrity and professional obligations." Johnson later said she "wasn't the right fit.".

"It’s yet another high-level change in the mayor’s administration and is a sign of continuing turmoil and a lack of direction at a very key time for the city, especially for him heading into a mayoral election," David Greising, CEO of the Better Government Association, told CBS Chicago after Gabrysch's abrupt exit.

According to recent reports, A survey of 1,108 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago, conducted Sept. 13-23, found that 22.2% approved of Johnson's job performance, while 52.9% disapproved and 24.8% had no opinion. The survey predates both the current petition review and Gabrysch's departure.

4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS.

Chicago residents are calling for more police as crime continues to rise in the Windy City. (Fox News Digital).

Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion 2027 budget is intended to close an $882.4 million gap, but a 28-member City Council bloc told him it did not see the votes needed to pass his tax proposals.

Standard & Poor's ultimately placed Chicago's BBB general-obligation rating on negative CreditWatch, citing the budget stalemate and management instability. The agency stated there was at least a 50% chance of a downgrade within 90 days, which could raise the city's borrowing costs.

The City Council eventually voted 45-5 on Wednesday to authorize an independent review of three years of financial reporting for possible material or intentional misstatements.

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks during a news conference March 25, 2026, in Chicago (AP Photo/Erin Hooley).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

Industry observers note that when U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have revealed a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

The relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of newly introduced export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

Since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept fresh tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

According to recent reports, beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

Industry observers note that so far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his tech giant’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And fresh U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

According to recent reports, although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

Industry observers note that prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

Beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

Sources indicate that another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the new historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

According to recent reports, but China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

Industry observers note that the awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

Sources indicate that if diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

To keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed newly introduced export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

Beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end people, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing indicated how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Sources indicate that beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

Sources indicate that the timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard launched water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

China has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued new gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

And around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

It has been revealed that outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

Beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set latest precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

According to recent reports, what looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several important questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

Sources indicate that the United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

It has been revealed that from the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to matter general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end consumers and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a upcoming category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

Beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

Recent findings suggest that tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

These headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

It has been revealed that if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

#99614. Latest Update: After ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ 5 of the Best Movies About the CIA

Latest Update: After ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ 5 of the Best Movies About the CIA

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
  • “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character.
  • In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

“You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

Recent findings suggest that “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

Industry observers note that but then again, Wild Horse Nine, set during the 1973 Chilean coup, isn’t really about the CIA. The dark comedy—a good bet for landing several Academy Award nominations—is about mortality and remorse and how even the most brazen people can have moments of clarity and reevaluate their past actions. It uses the CIA as a skin, the way McDonagh’s previous (and very similar) fatalistic comedy In Bruges did with contract killers.

Although its average employee likely has a job as mundane as any other government worker, an organization as key to world affairs and as necessarily shrouded in mystery as the CIA is understandably a great font for storytellers. But I can’t say there have been too many classic films that treat the CIA seriously.

In a recent development, there have been some marvelous paranoid thrillers, specifically Watergate-era classics like Three Days of the Condor, which tend to get a little far-fetched by the third act. There are some exceptions, like 2005’s Syriana and 2014’s A Most Wanted Man, that show the minutiae of spy craft in a compelling way that doesn’t devolve into silliness. These are rarities. I also don’t really consider Sicario or Zero Dark Thirty CIA films, because their sweep covers multiple government agencies.

The lengthy 2006 film The Good Shepherd, directed by Robert De Niro and starring Matt Damon, was an attempt to show how the agency grew out of Yale secret societies and reached a crisis point during the Bay of Pigs. Despite some good intentions, though, the movie is a significant dud and has few champions. (I recently revisited the film, but found myself needing several attempts, after I fell asleep on the couch on more than one occasion.).

Even for pure action-adventure absurdity, Britain has James Bond, but the United States has … James Bond’s friend Felix Leiter? Nice guy and all, but not 007. Mission: Impossible’s Ethan Hunt works for the Impossible Missions Force, remember, not the CIA. In the 1960s, Derek Flint, a Bond knockoff, worked for Z.O.W.I.E. (Zonal Organization World Intelligence Espionage), and Matt Helm worked for ICE (Intelligence and Counter-Espionage). Other than Jack Ryan, whose recent Amazon series and films have been absolutely horrible, Hollywood hasn’t given us a CIA man who’s become a household name.

There have, of course, been great movies about the CIA, but all of them are laced with comedy. Maybe this is some kind of national defense mechanism? Hey, don’t mind us, we may be tinkering in the affairs of other sovereign nations, but we know it’s a little naughty.

If the dark comedy of Wild Horse Nine has you itching for more examples of this curious phenomenon, here are five titles you can stream—all of which are intellectually zesty and a great deal of fun. (The Good Shepherd has value, too, should you find your stash of zolpidem depleted.) I’ve listed them from least-to-most zany.

Bryan Cranston and Ben Affleck in Argo.IMDB.

Sources indicate that this extremely watchable spy movie—with a healthy dose of comedy—was a major financial success and also won the Academy Award for best picture. (It beat both Steven Spielberg’s Lincoln and the aforementioned Zero Dark Thirty, both of which I’d place higher, but much like an operation to destabilize a country’s democracy, Oscar success isn’t always predictable.).

The story is rooted in a true event: During the Iran hostage crisis, a CIA agent (Affleck) created an elaborate cover story to smuggle home six Americans who were hiding with the Canadian ambassador. His cockamamie blueprint was to fake being a Canadian film production that was scouting for locations. To make it work, there had to be a real script (a Star Wars knockoff) plus actual Hollywood producers and craftspeople—so Alan Arkin and John Goodman (playing John Chambers, the real-life guy who did the prosthetics for Planet of the Apes) join in.

Naturally, there are setbacks and raised stakes as the baddies piece together which Americans are missing, then there’s a race against the clock for the massive finish. Sadly (well, not for the real people involved), the action-adventure elements of the last act were made up for the movie. But Argo is still an engrossing heist-style picture. It has respect for the CIA, but also presents an agency with a prankster’s edge.

Funnily enough, a 1966 crime-comedy from Italian director Vittorio De Sica and Newly introduced York playwright Neil Simon called After the Fox used the idea of a fake movie production as the cover for a grand scheme—but in their case, it was smuggling gold.

More recently, a group of Hollywood producers used the Argo technique as cover for an actual scheme in Poland, trying to recover a cache of stamps believed stolen from concentration camp prisoners. They even made a documentary film, The Stamp Thief, about the charade.

Julia Roberts and Tom Hanks in Charlie Wilson’s War. IMDB.

It has been revealed that in the months after 9/11, like many freaked-out Americans, I would stay up until dawn watching cable news stations, which is where I first learned the term “blowback,” and about how some felt that the CIA’s backing of the Mujahideen against the Soviets in Afghanistan caused a domino effect that eventually knocked down the Twin Towers. If I tried to explain what I’d seen the night before on C-SPAN 2, I sounded a bit like a paranoid lunatic, so I was very happy when screenwriter Aaron Sorkin and director Mike Nichols collaborated on Charlie Wilson’s War, a scathingly dark CIA satire that summed a lot of this up.

In a recent development, the always affable Tom Hanks stars as the sleazy titular congressman who, from a Vegas hot tub filled with Playboy models, sees a 60 Minutes report about Afghan refugees. It’s 1980, and he’s worried about Soviet encroachment, but also finds himself (somewhat to his surprise) genuinely caring about civilians caught up in large geopolitical events.

Sources indicate that he finds likeminded spirits in Joanne Herring (Julia Roberts), a wealthy Houston socialite and political activist, and Gust Avrakotos (Philip Seymour Hoffman), a working-class CIA operative with a brilliant mind, well-honed bullshit detector, and extremely short temper who was just passed over for promotion. Like Argo, Charlie Wilson’s War is practically a heist picture, but about pushing levers in Washington to quietly appropriate funds and bring matériel to the Afghan fighters.

Sources indicate that the dark punchline, of course, is how our heroes are powerless when it comes time to “win the peace,” as it were, leaving a power vacuum that, it can easily be argued, was filled by al Qaeda. The film’s release at the end of George W. Bush’s presidency functioned as a needed release valve.

Walter Matthau in Hopscotch.IMDB.

Quite the opposite of seductive Sean-Connery-as-007 is hangdog Walter Matthau, but the dark comedy Hopscotch suggests they have some traits in common. Matthau plays Miles Kendig, a veteran CIA agent whose boss (Ned Beatty) takes him out of the field and sticks him with a desk job. As revenge, Kendig decides he’ll write his memoirs (much like Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine), and his spilled secrets make security agencies across the globe very nervous. As he sends salacious excerpts to international higher-ups from various international hiding spots, one of the few things the CIA and KGB can agree upon is: Get Matthau away from his typewriter!

Aiding him is an old flame (Glenda Jackson, who also starred with Matthau’s in the popular comedy House Calls) who lives in Austria, which is a nice touch because our lead character is an opera nut who likes to sing along (poorly) to Mozart in the car.

What Hopscotch has in common with Charlie Wilson’s War is presenting CIA bosses as absolute buffoons. The best part is when Matthau uses Beatty’s own vacation home as a hideout—which America’s intelligence forces then shoot to pieces. While Walter Matthau circa 1980 isn’t the most athletic secret agent, he’s quick with disguises, voices, thinking on his feet, and laying out elaborate traps. This is a great old school comedy with just enough post-Watergate negativity to keep it sharp.

Alan Arkin and Peter Falk in The In-Laws.IMDB.

Hopscotch is a little wacky. The In-Laws is full-on madcap. It’s also one of the funniest movies ever made, though its serpentine plot is hard to explain in just a few sentences. But I’ll give it a go….

In a recent development, alan Arkin plays a nervous dentist whose daughter is getting married to a nice kid, but Arkin hasn’t yet met the boy’s family. Turns out the father, played by Peter Falk, is a noisy madman who is either bank robber or a rogue CIA agent with blockhead bosses in the middle of an elaborate scheme to overthrow a Latin American dictator. Things soon spiral out of control, and this odd couple find themselves in several high-speed chases, dodging bullets while still hoping to make it to the wedding in time. The two great actors zing each other with quality barbs, and when that’s been exhausted there’s some physical comedy, too.

According to recent reports, the screenplay, written by Andrew Bergman, who also worked on Blazing Saddles, Fletch, and Soapdish, offers a much milder version of the impudence toward the CIA that you see in Wild Horse Nine. “You win some, you lose some,” Peter Falk shrugs when asked about the Bay of Pigs. Though this movie is mostly a comedic joy, the notion that U.S. intelligence is in the hands of nutcases at best—or sheer incompetents at worst—finds quick purchase here and seems to have reverberated in the decades since.

Brad Pitt and Frances McDormand in Burn After Reading. IMDB.

There’s a lot about John Malkovich’s Wild Horse Nine character, Chris Carlisle, that may feel familiar. In Burn After Reading, the Coen brothers’ shaggiest movie (besides The Significant Lebowski), Malkovich plays Osborne Cox, a CIA agent who is demoted and decides to write a vicious memoir. But unlike the overlooked and pen-poised agents mentioned on this list already, Cox is a complete klutz.

But so is everyone in this tale, which includes Brad Pitt as dunderhead gym trainer Chad Feldheimer who, after a wild string of goof-ups and misunderstandings, ends up with a computer disc holding the first draft of Cox’s book. Feldheimer thinks he’s stumbled upon some serious material (it’s really just drunken grievances) and decides to blackmail Cox. This does not go well, and a ripple effect includes a murderer’s row of daffy performances from George Clooney, Frances McDormand, Richard Jenkins (more dumb than daffy), J.K. Simmons (exasperated by the stupidity around him, but powerless), and others.

Sources indicate that this was the Coen brothers’ follow-up to No Country For Old Men, their Oscar-winning crime drama based on Cormac McCarthy’s dark tale of greed and fate, and it’s probably the most cartoonish thing they’ve ever done. The CIA is nothing but a punching bag for 96 minutes, but the remaining undercurrent of violence erupts from time to time in some shocking (but hilarious) moments. Burn After Reading pushes the silliness to the absolute edge, but still somehow feels like parts of it could be true.

Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central Fresh Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman.

#99613. Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)

Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, warned that Congress’ 50 years of action have led Social Security to the cliff of insolvency.
  • A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that its reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.
  • Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that the group from a bygone era was right as the safety net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, warned that Congress’ 50 years of action have led Social Security to the cliff of insolvency.

A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that its reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.

Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that the group from a bygone era was right as the safety net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.

According to recent reports, "Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could.".

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme" and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.

AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS.

President Jimmy Carter shakes hands with Louisiana Sen. Russell Long after signing the Social Security bill at the White House in Washington on Dec. 20, 1977. (Getty Archive).

Johnson wrote in his report that, at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today.".

Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

In a recent development, "What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages, you're effectively building a solvency crisis into the program," Biggs said. "You are over-promising, you're going to build in benefits that the current system can't afford to pay and you're committing future taxpayers to pay rates of taxes that the taxpayers in 1977 weren't willing to pay.".

In the decades since, Congress has done little to change the program.

SENATE REPUBLICANS BREAK THROUGH WASHINGTON GRIDLOCK WITH MASSIVE AMERICAN ENERGY, DATA CENTER OVERHAUL.

Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, told Fox News Digital that’s largely because lawmakers have not had the political will to do it.

She agreed with Johnson that Social Security was effectively a "Ponzi scheme," and said "there's this misconception that a lot of Americans think that Social Security is a retirement savings program.".

It has been revealed that "But for that, you would actually need to have savings occur in the system, and there would need to be assets that would be invested in earning returns," Boccia mentioned. "That's not the case. We're talking about a pay-as-you-go program.".

One of the side effects of Congress’ lack of action to rein in the program is that the wage growth formula relies on workers in the economy contributing with their paychecks.

Boccia noted that as the decades have gone on, "we've seen a severe decline in the number of workers compared to the number of retirees collecting benefits as a result of a decline in fertility.".

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., makes his way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

Congress’ last real successful effort to reform Social Security came in the early 1980s, Biggs noted, when lawmakers were forced to step in to deal with the "funding crisis" hitting the program.

According to recent reports, "They raised taxes. They increased the retirement age. So, they did this with months to spare to fix Social Security," Biggs noted. "It's not something they wanted to do, but they were forced to do.

"Now, in 2032, we're going to face the same situation, where Congress will be forced to take action sometime before the trust fund runs out in 2032, not because they want to, but because they're forced to do it," he continued.

If Social Security’s trust fund runs dry by 2032, Americans’ benefits would be slashed, and the onus of paying for the shortfall would add trillions more to the nation’s debt.

It has been revealed that but Johnson, in his report, declared that the Social Security problem could not be fixed between now and then because of Congress’ inaction for the last several decades. And he suggested the solution would be to repeal a possible benefits reduction as the program’s trust fund heads toward insolvency in just under seven years.

Industry observers note that biggs, who was part of former President George W. Bush’s effort to reform Social Security over two decades ago, stated that, had Congress taken action "25 years ago, you could fix Social Security in barely noticeable ways.".

President Donald Trump said Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.

After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.

Sources indicate that speaking in a stuffy James A. Brady Briefing Room for just shy of 90 minutes, the GOP president contended, without naming a single Democratic leader or lawmaker, that members of the opposition party have called him “about two things in particular,” pointing to health care and immigration.

“What's happened is I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said of the 17 days since Democrats gained dozens of seats across the two chambers. “But people that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me.”.

But Trump also reminded Democrats that he is more than willing to veto legislation he doesn’t agree with, calling it one of the “extreme powers” of his office and one he might use to bring them to the bargaining table.

“So they’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things, and I’m going to veto them,” he mentioned. “I think, after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ’I’m going to veto, unless you want to do this and this and this.”.

He predicted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely new speaker of the House, and Sen. Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., expected to become majority leader, would seek deals because both are “smart.” He would not say if he’d spoken to either leader, but called Jeffries “streetwise,” while noting he had once made a donation to Schumer earlier in their careers.

Trump went as far as to suggest working across the aisle on health care “may be easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation,” a reference to a fast-track process that allows sprawling bills to pass each chamber with a simple majority — legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate.

The sports-loving president added the Senate-approved “Protect College Sports Act” to his list, and repeated his support for legislation to make Hollywood production companies more competitive. The House moved closer Friday to acting on an amended “Protect” bill when the Rules Committee posted a notice calling for any desired floor amendments by noon on Wednesday.

“We have to pass that bill,” Trump said. “Every college is going to go bankrupt if we don't get a bill because they're going crazy.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Senate’s “Protect” bill would establish the first federal regulatory framework for college athletics, setting national rules for name, image and likeness deals and compensation, as well as installing limitations on agents. It would put in place standards for NIL agreements, create guidelines for schools making direct payments to athletes and provide targeted antitrust protections to certain governing organizations.

In a recent development, he noted the Senate bill has “tremendous bipartisan support,” but its path in the House remains unclear, according to lobbyists who have worked on the issue. That’s because some House conservatives oppose it and the Congressional Black Caucus has said its members would vote “no.”.

The CBC has linked it to GOP efforts to redistrict majority minority districts in states the group, with its nearly 60 House members, contends would benefit most from the bill. The CBC is expected to be even larger in the next Congress, further complicating the “Protect” bill’s path to Trump’s desk.

In a recent development, trump also pointed to the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act as another possible bipartisan bill. The legislation would establish a federal tax credit to encourage film and television productions to shoot in the United States rather than overseas. Some countries offer American film companies lucrative production incentives to shoot on their soil.

According to recent reports, in a twist, Trump noted Sen. Adam B. Schiff — a longtime foe from the California Democrat’s days probing the president’s alleged ties to Russia as House Intelligence Committee chair during Trump 1.0 — supports that measure.

It has been revealed that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support. I tell you what, Adam Schiff noted, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’”.

But the president’s vision of a 120th Congress bipartisan agenda differs from what Democrats have promised.

Many Democratic incumbents and candidates promised voters they would pursue legislation to lower consumer prices, pare health care costs and end Trump’s Iran conflict, which the president again on Friday acknowledged hurt his party by increasing prices.

According to recent reports, jeffries, during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, pointed to reversing the administration’s Medicaid cuts, reviving the Affordable Care Act credits, ending the war and lowering costs as his conference’s “North Star” priorities. This week he also noted he would seek to move an immigration-related bill “immediately,” and that the House would “hold the crooks accountable,” a nod to aggressive oversight both chambers are likely to engage in.

In a recent development, on Iran, reporters pressed Vice President JD Vance over his post-midterms X post blaming the war for the GOP wipeout. One reporter pressed Vance, a potential 2028 Republican presidential hopeful, whether he — like Trump — would start the conflict again. Vance sidestepped as he approached the lectern from behind Trump’s right shoulder, but did not give a full-throated endorsement to go to war again.

According to recent reports, “The president has stated he would do it again,” Vance replied. “And my view is that my goal is, and my job is to support the president of the United States.”.

In a potential 2028 GOP primary preview, Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who has gained ground in some polls since the midterms — was expressionless as he stood a few feet away, positioned behind Trump’s left shoulder.

Trump’s midday press conference marked his first since voters handed Democrats at least 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate come Jan. 3. He again contended the outcome would have been different “if I were on the ballot,” and floated vague conspiracy theories about some falling prices since Democratic candidates bulldozed across the country.

In a recent development, at one point, he decided to make an announcement that he claimed he had not warned his staff about by floating a threat to U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas.

​"We're going to put a tremendous tax on them, if they do it," he noted, continuing his advocacy of erecting the unpopular facilities across the United States and willingness to use executive powers.

In a recent development, as he returned to Washington Thursday night, the White House touted on social media what it called $17 billion in fresh deals secured with Asian countries this week. Trump on Friday claimed he told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his country would begin buying “100 percent” of its oil from the United States — and Marcos had mentioned, “Yes, sir.”.

White House aides handed out a one-page “declaration toward peace” before Trump arrived that he later said he had reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

It has been revealed that trump called the declaration “formal,” as he lauded Chinese cities he was driven through this week as extremely “clean.” He compared them to some Democratic-run U.S. cities and states he described as “so embarrassing” and “dirty.” He dubbed Xi, considered by many Republican and Democratic lawmakers to be a dictator, a “great man.”.

Some Republican lawmakers who will return for the 120th Congress said they have some reservations about Trump meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, doubting Putin’s and Xi’s sincerity about changing course on a number of complications.

Recent findings suggest that “Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and to China. And Ronald Reagan is rolling in his grave. … And now the Democrats are talking about the bad Russians and the bad Chinese, and we got to be tougher — it’s another role reversal, here.”.
