#99610. America’s Hidden AI Advantage

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2254 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

America’s Hidden AI Advantage

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.
  • In the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy.
  • It has been revealed that this narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.

The United States—Not China—Dominates Diffusion.

In the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy. Even if the United States has a small lead in frontier AI models, the consensus is that China is better at applying the technology. As Kevin Rudd, former prime minister of Australia and a prominent observer of Chinese politics, declared at a conference in October, China is “miles ahead” in spreading AI “into the real economy.” This fits a familiar narrative about the technological rivalry between the two great powers: the United States innovates while China turns those innovations into practical applications at scale.

It has been revealed that this narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI. But it doesn’t match reality. After the Chinese startup DeepSeek shocked the world in early 2025 with the announcement of an open-source large language model that rivaled the capabilities of frontier models made by American companies, the international media published breathless reports on how DeepSeek’s model had rapidly spread across state-owned enterprises, hospitals, and provincial and local governments. Months later, however, analysts determined that this adoption was shallow, narrow, and slow; the technology was being used on clunky “all-in-one machines” embedded on isolated hardware units within these institutions, rather than integrated more broadly into the software services they were using. Then, in January 2026, outside observers marveled at OpenClaw, a fresh open-source AI agent, as a sign of China’s diffusion advantage. Now, the excitement about these open-source agents has dissipated as security vulnerabilities and inefficiency have limited their uptake.

According to recent reports, it is the United States, not China, that has a decisive lead in AI diffusion. This is because the United States has comparative advantages in both its overall level of economic development and the nature of its growth model. China’s underdeveloped software market, weak technology transfer mechanisms, and centralized economic system make AI diffusion much more challenging. All told, the United States’ advantage in diffusing the technology through the economy is likely to persist for the foreseeable future.

Recent findings suggest that despite its reputation as a pioneer of digital technology such as cashless payments and messaging apps, China’s overall digitization levels—the extent to which software and other digital tools have penetrated various sectors of the economy—are far lower than those in the United States. American firms are on average more than twice as likely as their Chinese competitors to adopt cloud computing services. And the U.S. enterprise software market, which includes services to manage customer relationships and provide business intelligence, is approximately ten times larger than China’s. According to the 2022 Global Cloud Ecosystem Index, which ranked 76 countries on their access to and usage of cloud services, China sat in the bottom half; the United States, by contrast, ranked 17th, not far behind the top performers, in part because of its dominance of “software as a service” products in which businesses can gain access to enterprise software without needing to install and maintain the programs themselves.

China’s relatively low penetration of digital services is a barrier to diffusing AI. When small Chinese hospitals tried to adopt DeepSeek, for instance, they lacked information systems that could collect and manage the data necessary to take full advantage of AI models. In these hospitals, which include many small health facilities in rural areas, patient data is still recorded on paper; where digital records do exist, they are often incomplete or vary from hospital to hospital. By contrast, 95 percent of U.S. doctors maintain electronic health record systems in their offices. As a result, U.S. hospitals have more smoothly integrated AI into electronic health records to recommend treatments, predict health risks, and simplify billing.

China’s underdeveloped cloud and enterprise software ecosystem also explains why the OpenClaw hype did not translate to sustainable diffusion. Open-source tools like OpenClaw appeal to hobbyists and individual developers who are keen to experiment and are less sensitive to security issues. But small businesses have been slow to adopt such tools because they prefer reliable, standardized solutions that are easy to implement and patch. Small businesses are more likely to rely on cloud-based tools and enterprise software to implement AI upgrades than to try to experiment on their own—two channels that are less robust in China than in the United States.

The United States also has an advantage over China because of linkages within the science and technology ecosystem that help disseminate advances. Collaboration between universities and businesses is critical to diffusing AI breakthroughs across the entire economy because these connections bring together innovators who can develop new AI products and implementers who can effectively commercialize them.

According to recent reports, in this dimension, the United States is far ahead of China. Americans have long led the world in the publication of articles about AI co-authored by at least one researcher from academia and one researcher from industry. Between 2015 and 2019, U.S. researchers published more than twice as many such articles as their Chinese counterparts. The gap extends beyond AI: across the life sciences and natural sciences, the share of publications in the United States that involved both university and industry researchers was also more than double the comparable rate in China. Beijing recognizes this gap: China’s official state news agency ranked weak technical exchanges between industry and academia as one of the five crucial shortcomings of the country’s AI ecosystem.

According to recent reports, although Chinese policymakers are aware of this challenge and have promoted policies to try to spur collaboration between universities and businesses, especially in AI, it will be difficult to cultivate the requisite trust needed for these two sectors to work together. China’s weak intellectual property protections, for example, discourage universities from pursuing partnerships with industry actors because they fear losing ownership of their inventions. The United States, by contrast, has a tradition of university-industry collaboration. The 1980 Bayh-Dole Act, which provides incentives and patent protections that encourage universities to commercialize inventions and license them to the private sector, kick-started decades of collaboration. Without a similar connective tissue to link academic institutions and businesses, Chinese universities are not as equipped to form profitable partnerships with companies. Chinese technical and engineering education is also disconnected from commercial enterprises, meaning that schools do not teach students the specific skills that companies need in their workforces.

Weak technology transfer mechanisms also undermine one of China’s main strengths in AI diffusion: its massive talent base. Analysis by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation showed that in 2022, China awarded around 50,000 doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and math, compared with only about 34,000 in the United States. Although the sheer quantity of Chinese computer science graduates may eventually help the country adopt AI advances at scale, the quality of that education determines how promptly or effectively education can encourage AI diffusion. If training is divorced from practical applications, graduates will struggle to adapt cutting-edge advances from industry labs into the sectors in which they work. Consider one commonly used standard to measure the baseline quality of AI education: whether a university employs at least one researcher who has published at least one paper at a leading AI conference. According to data from 2023–24, only 38 universities in China met this standard; the United States accounted for 150.

In a recent development, china’s centrally planned approach to AI development is also counterproductive when it comes to diffusion. In 2025, China developed an “AI Plus” action plan that outlines targets for AI adoption over the next decade and released guidelines for government agencies and local officials on how to put the plan into effect across the country. For many observers, the mere existence of a plan showed that the highest levels of Chinese leadership were committed to spreading AI widely and that China was better positioned to win the AI race than the United States, which lacks any kind of similar diffusion blueprint. Rudd’s claims about China’s edge in AI adoption, for instance, cite Beijing’s ambitious policies and targets for AI diffusion as supporting evidence.

In a recent development, but centralized approaches such as China’s often impede technology diffusion, especially when the state tries to intervene in domains in which the development trajectory is uncertain. One of the planks of China’s AI Plus blueprint identifies “global cooperation” as a priority sector for AI adoption. If local governments were to implement the plan as outlined, it would shift resources from areas in which diffusion has been proven to be effective, such as health care, to the undefined space of “global cooperation.” More broadly, Beijing’s favoritism toward state-owned enterprises and its preference for picking national champions often prop up inefficient technologies that would have been weeded out by market-based competition. Other businesses are unlikely to adopt inefficient technologies, making nonmarket forms of AI development less likely to diffuse widely.

Counterintuitively, the lack of a clear U.S. policy on AI diffusion is a boon, not a hindrance, to the United States’ attempt to diffuse the technology across the economy. At the height of U.S.-Japanese competition in the 1980s, for instance, when the two countries were racing to train software engineers who could spread computer technology, Japan’s Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture, as it was then known, exercised centralized control over universities. But emerging trends in computer science developed faster than the government could adapt. By concentrating state funds on centers of excellence and imposing one-size-fits-all rules on the computing curriculum, Japan could not match the adaptability of American universities, and the United States surged ahead. Cross-national studies have shown that decentralized science and technology systems are correlated with faster diffusion of latest innovations.

Another historical case with parallels to China, the Soviet Union, further suggests how centralization is antithetical to diffusion. In the twentieth century, the Soviet Union boasted many plans for technology development. Yet its top-down approach, which focused on large-scale engineering projects, undercut market-based instruments that encourage technology diffusion through competition. As a result, although the Soviet Union pioneered fresh technologies in many areas, including the casting of steel, it fell behind the United States in adopting general-purpose technologies such as computers. A prescient U.S. intelligence report published in 1969 deemed the Soviet Union’s mechanisms for technology diffusion as “much more balky” than those of the United States because of the absence of competitive pressures as well as limited linkages between the R & D system and the broader economy.

The myth of China’s lead in AI diffusion persists despite clear data showing U.S. advantages. In part, this may be because China’s innovation system has facilitated the widespread adoption of certain visible technologies. In less than 20 years, China has built more than 30,000 miles of high-speed rail, for example, blanketing the country with ultra-fast trains that now reach even the most remote provinces.

Industry observers note that but infrastructure presents a very different challenge than AI does. The centralized pressure that officials can use to effectively develop large-scale infrastructure projects is much less effective for general-purpose technologies like AI because it is infeasible to mandate that all small- and medium-size firms, spread across every sector of the economy, adopt artificial intelligence. Those companies would do so only if it made sense from a business perspective, and few have the digital foundations or savvy employees able to harness AI in a way that would help them grow. Moreover, the United States has outbuilt China in the infrastructure most essential to AI development, data centers, in which it retains a ten-to-one edge. In fact, in some cases, the data centers that China has built remain idle because of weak AI demand.

According to recent reports, the misperception that China leads AI diffusion may continue unabated because analysis of the country’s technology ecosystem is overly focused on frontier firms such as ByteDance and DeepSeek and first-tier cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai. Yet AI diffusion ultimately rests on whether adoption occurs in medium size companies, small towns, and inland provinces, where it has been extremely limited. Because these settings rarely feature in outside media coverage, analysis of China’s AI diffusion landscape underestimates the difficulty of translating cutting-edge advances from frontier labs and universities in Hangzhou or Shenzhen to, say, a small firm in a county seat in northwestern Qinghai Province.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the simplest explanation is that such a myth is useful, even if ultimately untrue. In some ways, the United States is trumpeting Beijing’s AI diffusion in the way that Chinese “tiger parents” try to motivate their children to work harder by raising the success of “that other family’s kid.” “Look at how well that other family’s kid performed at the piano recital,” they might say, without listening closely to ensure that the notes were exactly right. In great-power rivalry, too, there is a natural tendency to overhype the other side’s capabilities, in part to spur more effort at home.

But such a “useful” myth can backfire if it pushes the United States to overlook its own advantages or even to mimic China’s more top-down approach to AI development. By any measure, the United States maintains a comfortable lead in AI diffusion, and China, despite its impressive successes, has serious challenges. Although the narrative of Chinese dominance endures, for now all signs point to a U.S. lead that will remain strong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate judicial confirmations accelerate, and Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., breaks down the Republican strategy before Democrats take control of the chamber.

Incoming Senate Republican campaign Chairman Bernie Moreno claims the party faces a "very tough" road ahead as the GOP aims to take back its majority in 2028 after taking significant losses in the midterms earlier this month.

Industry observers note that democrats convincingly grabbed control of the Senate and will hold a 56-44 majority when the latest Congress is sworn in at the start of the new year. They also won control of the House, and multiple governors' seats flipped from red to blue.

In the Senate, the latest split means Republicans will need to flip at least six seats in the 2028 elections to win back the majority. That number rises to seven seats if they lose the White House in the next election cycle.

SENATE REPUBLICANS FEAR 'BRUTAL' 2028 MAP COULD KEEP DEMOCRATS IN POWER FOR YEARS.

One senator told Fox News Digital Republicans can "forget 2028.".

"It is an absolutely brutal map," Moreno recently told Fox News Digital, pointing to the states up for grabs in 2028.

It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, will take over in January as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which is the Senate GOP's campaign arm. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

But the first-term senator from Ohio added that, in "politics, things change pretty promptly.".

At the start of the 2026 cycle, the Democrats faced a steep and narrow path to winning back the majority, but, by Election Day, the party was able to ride a massive blue wave formed by a favorable political climate to flip nine Senate seats.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, looking ahead to the next election, stated in an interview on Fox News' "America Reports, "We can come back. We will.".

"I've been there before, and we just have to get out and win the hearts and minds of the American people," Thune added. "And that means coming up with a compelling economic message, talking about secure streets, secure border, safe streets and more money in your pocket. I mean, I think those are the things that the American people care the most about.".

Looking ahead to the next two years, when he will be leading the GOP minority in the Senate, Thune remarked, "We now have an opportunity in the minority to draw those bold lines, those contrasts, and make sure that we are delivering a message that connects with the middle of the electorate.".

Recent findings suggest that in 2028, Republicans will need to hold onto seats in battlegrounds Wisconsin and North Carolina, where GOP Sens. Ron Johnson and Ted Budd are up for re-election.

Meanwhile, Republicans will work to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and Maggie Hassan of Fresh Hampshire.

TRUMP GRIP ON GOP FACES MAJOR POST-ELECTION TEST.

In a recent development, sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., makes his way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

Fetterman, who has repeatedly broken with his party and seen his poll numbers among Democrats crater, faces all-but-certain primary challenges if he seeks re-election. Kelly and Warnock are mulling White House runs in 2028.

Senate showdowns will also be held in 2028 in six states that President Donald Trump carried by double-digits two years ago that become key battlegrounds in this year's midterms.

Among them are Ohio, where former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown won a ticket back to the Senate with a five-point victory over appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted. Brown will fill out the final two years of Vice President JD Vance's old Senate term, so he'll face re-election in 2028.

Republicans will be defending seats in four states where Democrats scored Senate flips in this year's midterms. The four seats are held by GOP Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, Jerry Moran of Kansas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Tim Scott of South Carolina,.

Sources indicate that in Florida, appointed Republican Sen. Ashley Moody narrowly defeated progressive Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special election. Moody, who is filling out Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate term, will face re-election in two years.

House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

According to recent reports, according to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

Recent findings suggest that “House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat said in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. “They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he stated. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’".

#99603. The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1841 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent.
  • Although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics.

Recent findings suggest that in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

Although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

It has been revealed that south Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

Recent findings suggest that not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole new networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

Sources indicate that according to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

According to recent reports, but recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

Much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing upcoming. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

To safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

Sources indicate that seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

According to recent reports, but even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no aims to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

In a recent development, at first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

It has been revealed that yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

Sources indicate that still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

Yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

According to recent reports, seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating latest security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

But on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it reveals how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more notable, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the South Korean government was known to be considering developing nuclear weapons.

Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

Sources indicate that hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light reveals. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

Recent findings suggest that hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light shows. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

But perhaps the makers of Lioness deserve some credit simply for tackling the subject. Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, cultural depictions of how the war is actually being fought are strikingly thin on the ground. A few journalists have written solid first-person accounts of the conflict, and documentary filmmakers, many of them Ukrainian, have explored it with astonishing intimacy. Yet their works have reached relatively small audiences. Where are the gripping stories for the broader public?

According to recent reports, combat drones have certainly made a mark on the broader culture. You see them everywhere, from movies like The Terminal List: Dark Wolf , where an assassin uses a drone to blow up a car, to the BBC’s police procedural Vigil, which includes a sequence in which military drones are turned against their own side by a hostile hacker. It’s striking how often drones turn up in dystopian science fiction films—such as The Gorge, where two snipers fight off autonomous drones, and The Outer Threat, in which a man with a dramatic secret has to protect his family from a hostile government equipped with drone swarms. A few years ago, the drone designs in these films probably would have resembled the exquisitely engineered aircraft of the so-called global war on terror. Now, even sci-fi creators seem to be favoring small quadcopters like the ones used by Ukrainians in their fight against Russia. But few of these cultural references involve depictions of war.

It has been revealed that retired Australian Army Maj. Gen. Mick Ryan, who has carefully tracked the war in Ukraine, argues that pop culture can be a useful way of helping politicians and the public stay abreast of developments on the battlefield. “Military doctrine is inaccessible to most people, including a lot of people in the military,” he noted. “Whether it’s movies, television, books, or podcasts, [pop culture] can be an excellent way of making complex military and technological intersections accessible to a broader range of people.” Ryan practices what he preaches: He’s written an excellent speculative novel, White Sun War, about a hypothetical conflict over Taiwan, which includes detailed scenes of Chinese and U.S. forces fighting with the help of autonomous unmanned ground vehicles. Ryan’s fictional technology is ahead of what the Russians and Ukrainians have developed in their war—but only slightly.

A Ukrainian soldier fires at a drone flying overhead in Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on Nov. 11. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images.

Sources indicate that could it be that drone warfare is just too complicated for compelling storytelling? By now, both sides in the Russia-Ukraine war have deployed a wide variety of drones on land, at sea, and in the air. None of these machines exists in isolation. They’re part of complex battlefield ecosystems that encompass reconnaissance, strike, and (increasingly) supply. Lately the Ukrainians have even been using ground drones to evacuate wounded soldiers. The intensity of the conflict has driven an astonishing pace of innovation, often involving the intricacies of maintaining reliable communications and targeting in environments saturated with electronic warfare measures. Responses have included drones controlled by fiber-optic cables (which can’t be jammed, unlike radio signals) and increasing reliance on artificial intelligence systems that can keep drones on target even when their links with operators go down.

Perhaps it’s no surprise that outsiders have a hard time keeping up. In October, video game publisher Activision released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment of its long-running franchise. (A reminder: The global gaming industry is way bigger than the movie industry.) The story revolves around an imagined North Korean invasion of South Korea, and its depiction of the intense combat that such a conflict would entail is amazingly convincing. The game’s creators have put a huge amount of effort into getting the details right (even extending to hiring a dialect coach to consult on the different forms of Korean spoken by the characters).

It has been revealed that seeing the effort the game’s designers put into verisimilitude, it’s all the more surprising that drones have a very limited role. This omission is especially odd given that North Korea has dispatched large numbers of troops to help Russia in the war against Ukraine—in part so that Kim Jong Un’s forces could learn about the intricacies of drone warfare. The game’s creators seem to have been oblivious to this. When a joint South Korean-U.S. force counters the invasion with an amphibious counterattack, the intensity of the combat recalls the opening scenes of Saving Private Ryan. Yet neither side in the fight deploys drones on land or in the sky—although this is exactly the sort of combat in which modern militaries are already working frantically to incorporate the lessons of Ukraine.

In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of upcoming technologies.

From the president on down, many Americans still do not grasp the implications of drones and other threats.

Recent findings suggest that part of the problem is surely that the remote-controlled, seemingly anonymous nature of modern drones diminishes their narrative potential. Real-life drone operations often involve long and meticulous searches and extended loitering—not exactly the stuff of high drama. Those brutal Ukrainian drone attack videos that now populate social media show only the climactic moments that follow hours and hours of painstaking preparation and reconnaissance. This could be why we see some video game designers creating drones with machine guns on them; in real life, that’s a generally useless approach, since the recoil from the guns would destabilize the drone, perhaps fatally. But shooting feels a lot more satisfying than hitting a distant target that you can only see on a screen.

In a recent development, that video games present such a distorted vision of contemporary war is especially ironic considering that the gaming industry has significantly shaped drone warfare. Military drone controllers are often modeled on the ones used by gamers, which hugely simplifies training.

In a recent development, ukrainian filmmakers have found themselves confronting similar narrative challenges. The fascinating newly introduced movie Killhouse, which was shot in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military, features plenty of scenes that convey a vivid sense of the peculiarities of drone warfare. The film turns on the fate of a civilian couple who are lured into the gray zone between the front lines by Russian gangsters who are holding their daughter for ransom. Unlike the blissful U.S. soldiers in Lioness, the desperate mother and father are immediately detected by both the Russians and Ukrainians as soon as they enter the area. The Russians swiftly shell them, while the Ukrainians devise a complicated, drone-assisted plan for their rescue—and, ultimately, the daughter’s. One particularly nail-biting sequence depicts an operator trying to use a drone to guide a character through a minefield, even though he has no clear way of communicating with her.

The movie’s creators would have done well to stop there, after showing us real-life drones in real-life situations. Unfortunately, even they apparently felt the need to juice up their story by introducing a set of as-yet-non-existent drones that use facial recognition systems for their targets. (That capability is pretty useful for the Chinese surveillance state; why you would need it on a battlefield without expansive access to a database of enemy faces remains unclear.) At the moment of a critical showdown, these ultra-high-tech drones are used simply as brute force to knock out several Russian soldiers—all that fancy equipment ends up effectively serving the same purpose as a couple of major rocks.

Perhaps the shortcomings of movies and video games aren’t worth taking so seriously. There’s no requirement for ultra-realism, and no one should exaggerate the extent to which popular culture drives the decisions of policymakers. But is it just a coincidence that Western militaries, policymakers, and politicians are still failing to learn from the war in Ukraine after all these years?

A still from Killhouse. Ukrainian Film Division.

U.S. and other Western military bases are still plagued by drone incursions of unknown provenance; the one thing that’s clear is that many of these drones, which are equipped to resist powerful jamming, aren’t operated by hobbyists. In recent weeks, the U.S. Air Force has cited the threat of drone attacks in connection with at least two major alerts at air bases in Britain. Decision-makers were apparently reacting to fears that Iran might launch an attack emulating Kyiv’s stunning Operation Spiderweb, when Ukraine managed to destroy a number of Russian strategic bombers by launching drones that were smuggled into Russia on freight trucks. European NATO members have experienced various drone incursions, as well as confronting actual attacks. Even the Australians have had to deal with mysterious drone sightings near their bases. The technology is proliferating; the problem can no longer be written off.

According to recent reports, we’re still waiting for the Hollywood blockbuster that brings home the impact of drone warfare to ordinary voters—something like the 1927 film Wings, one of the first to familiarize a broad audience with the significance of military aircraft. But the lack of popular familiarity with the changed nature of war is no excuse for the complacency of Western leaders.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

It has been revealed that “Washington has a spending problem, and it indicates up in places major and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., mentioned Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”.

Hill stated in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still problem special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

According to recent reports, but the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

Recent findings suggest that as the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”.

How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicist and energy researcher Oliver Hemmers explains the engineering failures and economic challenges behind the collapse of Nevada’s billion-dollar Crescent Dunes solar plant.

It has been revealed that TONOPAH, Nev. — An Obama-era solar power plant once hailed as a "clean energy marvel" and backed by more than $1 billion in federal support has gone bankrupt for a second time and sold for just $7 million with the estimated taxpayer tab potentially reaching $507.6 million.

Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower.

The plant was designed to generate solar electricity even after sunset, using an emerging technology that promised to revolutionize green energy in America.

The Obama administration bet big on the project, backing it with a $737 million federal loan guarantee and around $275 million in Treasury grant awards as part of its broader $90 billion push to combat climate change and stimulate the economy after the 2008 financial crisis.

OBAMA-ERA 'CLEAN ENERGY' SOLAR POWER PLANT STILL USES FOSSIL FUELS – AND KILLS THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY.

The Crescent Dunes solar plant's central tower appears unlit, left, and illuminated by reflected sunlight, right. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital; Getty Images).

But the promise never matched the performance.

After operations began in late 2015, leaks and equipment failures repeatedly knocked the plant offline, production fell short and cheaper solar alternatives undercut its economics, driving the project into financial ruin and leaving taxpayers shouldering the cost.

The financial collapse comes 15 years after Solyndra, another Obama-backed solar company, went bankrupt and left taxpayers in the red for $528 million, a sum Crescent Dunes' estimated taxpayer tab could nearly match.

In a recent development, "The Crescent Dunes solar project is a microcosm of what is wrong with Democrat governance: the Green Upcoming Scam, hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars wasted, fraud and a cover-up," Rep. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital.

OBAMA-BACKED $2.2B GREEN ENERGY 'BOONDOGGLE' LEAVES TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK.

Recent findings suggest that president Barack Obama signs the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act as Vice President Joe Biden looks on in Denver, Colo., Feb. 17, 2009. The legislation helped finance the Obama administration's push into renewable energy, including the federal loan program that backed the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images).

Crescent Dunes sits about 13 miles northwest of the old mining town of Tonopah, roughly halfway between Las Vegas and Reno.

The isolated facility, which Fox News Digital toured, is surrounded by miles of barren desert, scrubland and distant mountain ranges.

Across the 2,250-acre federal site, more than 10,000 giant mirrors surround a 640-foot tower, the centerpiece of a system designed to overcome one of solar power's biggest limitations: darkness.

It has been revealed that unlike ordinary solar panels, which convert sunlight directly into electricity, Crescent Dunes focuses the sun's rays onto a receiver atop the tower, heating molten salt to roughly 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit. The salt stores that heat in a massive insulated tank, allowing it to produce steam that drives an electricity-generating turbine long after sunset.

That combination made it the first commercial-scale U.S. solar tower to use molten salt to both collect and store the sun's heat. DOE projected it would generate 482,000 megawatt-hours annually, with a maximum output of 110 megawatts, enough to supply more than 75,000 Nevada homes during peak periods.

Industry observers note that the Crescent Dunes solar plant uses more than 10,000 mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that stores energy. The stored heat is used to produce steam, drive a turbine and generate electricity, including after sunset. (Fox News).

SolarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

American developer SolarReserve developed the project, while Spanish contractor Cobra, a subsidiary of construction giant ACS Group, built it.

Both held ownership stakes in the organization that owned the plant, Tonopah Solar Energy.

Spanish banking giant Banco Santander also held an ownership stake in Tonopah Solar Energy.

Late Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., championed the project. In 2016, he called it an "engineering and clean energy marvel" and predicted that "Nevada will benefit for decades.".

The project reflected the Obama administration's push to expand clean energy by using taxpayer-backed financing to help bring promising but commercially risky technologies to market.

But Crescent Dunes demonstrated how expensive those gambles could become when they failed.

Crescent Dunes' problems emerged almost immediately.

A major leak in its molten-salt storage tank occurred in October 2016, less than a year after commercial operations began.

During that shutdown, Treasury approved a cash-grant payment in March 2017 under the Obama-era stimulus program, funding that later became the subject of serious fraud allegations.

It went back online in July 2017, but restarting the plant did not resolve its performance problems.

Even in 2018, its best full year through 2025, Crescent Dunes generated just 41% of the annual electricity output projected by DOE, according to federal energy records.

Then another tank failure halted generation in March 2019.

Seven months later, the repeated breakdowns and poor performance eventually cost Crescent Dunes its sole electricity customer when NV Energy terminated its 25-year agreement.

Without its long-term power contract, Crescent Dunes spiraled into financial trouble, culminating in its first bankruptcy in July 2020.

Recent findings suggest that the 2020 restructuring handed ownership to ACS through its affiliate, Crescent Dunes Investment, with Cobra running the plant. The turnaround plan counted on extensive repairs restoring production to 400,000 megawatt-hours a year, more than twice its best annual output.

The hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

According to recent reports, A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nev. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

The plant restarted in July 2021, only for further molten-salt tank leaks in 2022 and 2023 to force additional shutdowns.

Although the plant resumed selling electricity under shorter-term agreements, it continued to lose money and relied on financial support from affiliated companies, court records show.

REGULATORS ALLOW OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT TO KILL THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY, INVESTIGATION FINDS.

By January 2026, it was back in bankruptcy court. This time, the billion-dollar plant went on the auction block.

Mississippi-based Sons of Liberty Construction, a company owned by three brothers, bought it for $7 million in July and are attempting to revive it.

The plant was generating electricity during Fox News Digital's visit, although they mentioned it remained well below its initial intended output. Their efforts to restore the troubled facility are examined in Part 3 of this series.

It has been revealed that A timeline of the Crescent Dunes solar plant reveals major equipment failures in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2023, along with federal financing, Treasury grant approval, two bankruptcies and the project's eventual $7 million sale in July 2026. (Fox News).

Behind that history of breakdowns and bankruptcies lies a dispute over what failed: the solar technology, the construction behind it or a combination of both.

Bill Gould, SolarReserve's co-founder and former chief technology officer, blamed the project's Spanish construction contractor, ACS Cobra.

"It was a tragedy of mismanagement," Gould told Bloomberg in 2020, accusing the contractor of delaying necessary work and designing a defective molten-salt tank.

According to recent reports, an unnamed engineer who said he had worked at Crescent Dunes since its early development offered a similar account, blaming the tank failures on design and welding problems. He told SolarPACES in 2023 that the plant's solar collection technology had experienced comparatively few problems.

"It's just the old tech that's having these troubles," the engineer remarked, referring to the conventional thermal-power equipment.

The sheer size of the storage system posed a significant challenge, according to Oliver Hemmers, a physicist and energy researcher who formerly led the Harry Reid Center for Environmental Studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

"Ultimately, the larger you make those tanks that hold the molten salt, the harder the material science challenges become," Hemmers told Fox News Digital.

In a recent development, hemmers stated temperature swings of hundreds of degrees can cause the metal to repeatedly expand and contract, eventually creating cracks and leaks. He had not reviewed the plant's engineering plans but questioned whether the developers had sufficiently tested the tank design.

Sources indicate that "You need to have alloys that can withstand that heat variation without moving much. Otherwise, when the walls move, the vessel breaks, cracks and leaks. So, I'm not sure how much research they really put into the vessel design," he stated.

Hemmers noted that Crescent Dunes relied on a massive molten-salt storage tank, while other solar thermal facilities have used multiple smaller tanks to reduce the stresses caused by repeated heating and cooling.

Court records show how efforts to prevent further failures came at a cost.

Recent findings suggest that when the plant resumed operations in July 2023, operators lowered the hot-salt tank's temperature from its original design level of about 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit to about 850 degrees. They later raised it to as high as 900 degrees, but the lower temperatures still reduced electricity production and revenue.

Industry observers note that A 2015 Department of Energy promotional poster touts the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada, highlighting its $737 million federal loan guarantee and projected annual electricity generation of 482,000 megawatt-hours. The plant later suffered repeated equipment failures and two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (U.S. Department of Energy).

The receiver atop the 640-foot solar tower at Crescent Dunes glows as mirrors concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada, in August 2026. The troubled plant was sold for $7 million after its second bankruptcy earlier that year. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

As Crescent Dunes struggled to meet its production targets, competing solar technology was getting cheaper.

Falling prices for conventional solar panels, known as photovoltaic panels, including those manufactured in China, undercut the project.

Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, offering a simpler and increasingly cheaper way to generate solar power.

In a recent development, crescent Dunes, by contrast, uses more than 10,000 computer-controlled mirrors, called heliostats, to focus sunlight onto a receiver atop its central tower. The heat warms molten salt, which is then used to produce steam that drives turbines to generate electricity.

The mirrored faces of heliostats at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nev. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a receiver atop the plant's central tower, heating molten salt used to store thermal energy. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Recent findings suggest that crescent Dunes, however, has one key advantage. Its molten-salt storage system allows it to generate electricity even after sunset, something conventional solar panels cannot do without additional storage.

Recent findings suggest that those same economic pressures have battered California's Ivanpah solar plant, another Obama-era project Fox News Digital reported on that uses thousands of heliostats to concentrate sunlight. Unlike Crescent Dunes, Ivanpah cannot store the sun's heat to generate electricity after dark.

Fox News Digital contacted ACS Group and its attorneys but received no response.

The project was backed by more than $1 billion in federal loan guarantees and grants.

Industry observers note that that included a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee. DOE mentioned it resolved its financial interests in the project through the plant's first bankruptcy settlement in 2020 in an effort to maximize taxpayer recovery and estimated its loss on the loan at $232 million, a figure the department confirmed to Fox News Digital on background.

The Trump administration's Department of Energy blasted the handling of taxpayer money behind the project.

"It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green Fresh Scam. Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project," DOE assistant press secretary Caroline Murzin told Fox News Digital in a written statement.

The project also received a $275.6 million Treasury grant award, which, unlike the loan, was not intended to be repaid provided the project met the program's requirements.

Combined, the Treasury grant awards and DOE's estimated loan loss would put the total federal cost at approximately $507.6 million, although Treasury has not confirmed the full grant was disbursed and DOE has not provided a final accounting of its loan losses.

Fox News Digital has filed Freedom of Information Act requests with both the Energy and Treasury departments seeking a full accounting of the federal loans, grant payments and taxpayer losses associated with Crescent Dunes.

Rows of computer-controlled heliostats surround the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nev. The mirrors track the sun and direct concentrated sunlight toward the receiver atop the tower. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nev., while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

It has been revealed that the Treasury grant also became the focus of a private investor-backed lawsuit alleging that companies involved in construction fraudulently secured the money. A judge dismissed the case at DOJ's request, and the investors are appealing.

The allegations and the fight over the dismissal are examined in Part 2.

Reid, who died in 2021, had championed Crescent Dunes as a showcase for government and private industry working together to build "the next generation of clean energy technology.".

Its financial collapse has sharpened the question behind that partnership: Should taxpayers bankroll commercially risky energy projects that private lenders are unwilling to fully finance?

"The government shouldn't be picking winners and losers," Véronique de Rugy, an economist at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, told Fox News Digital.

Recent findings suggest that "This is not the role of the government. The government is not good at actually picking projects that somehow the private sector is leaving on the sidewalk," she said.

It has been revealed that de Rugy argued that politicians take credit for publicly financed projects without facing the same consequences when they collapse. Unlike private investors, she said, politicians don't personally bear the financial losses when their bets go wrong.

"So, then they can go and do a ribbon-cutting ceremony when the plant opens, and then they're usually nowhere to be seen when the company goes under," she remarked.

She also argued that many companies receiving government assistance would have succeeded without it, questioning why taxpayers should shoulder the risks of commercial investments.

Recent findings suggest that "These subsidies go to projects that end up failing, right? Then taxpayers have to shoulder the bill," she mentioned.

Nick Loris, president of the Conservative Coalition for Climate Solutions (C3 Solutions), a conservative energy and environmental policy think tank, offered a different perspective, arguing that government financing can sometimes justify the risks of developing fresh technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "I wouldn't call it a mistake. I think it took a risky bet on a potentially promising technology that aimed to solve one of the challenges with solar in its intermittency," Loris told Fox News Digital.

He argued that federal financing can help promising technologies reach the market when private investors are reluctant to take the risk, and that failures such as Crescent Dunes should be weighed against successful projects and interest earnings across DOE's broader loan portfolio.

In a recent development, one example is California's Desert Sunlight, a 550-megawatt solar farm that uses panels instead of mirrors and molten salt. In a 2024 assessment, DOE noted the project helped prove the viability of large-scale solar and was meeting its loan obligations.

Recent findings suggest that across the broader program, DOE reported in its fiscal 2027 budget justification that borrowers had paid nearly $5 billion in interest, compared with nearly $1 billion in default losses, through Sept. 30, 2025.

But Hemmers questioned whether Crescent Dunes ever made economic sense, arguing that the billion-dollar investment was a risky gamble from the outset.

It has been revealed that "Right, we kind of say, 'OK, that was a boondoggle. It didn't work.' And, so, now we move on, right, do something else," Hemmers mentioned.

The Paradox of American Credibility
