📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that JOSHUA A. SCHWARTZ is Assistant Professor of International Relations and Emerging Technology at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.

How Fighting Weakens Washington’s Reputation—and Backing Down May Strengthen It.

It has been revealed that in mid-February, after the United States failed to get Iran to renounce its nuclear ambitions, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an ultimatum. The Iranian leadership had to make “a meaningful deal” with Washington. “Otherwise,” he remarked, “bad things happen.” Barely eight days later, the United States and Israel began the war against Iran that continues today.

That war has been criticized on many grounds, but analysts have often overlooked the basic assumption about U.S. credibility that it has tested. There is a long-held understanding that the United States’ willingness to use force to stand up for its interests is essential to deterring future adversaries—and convincing them to give in to the kind of sweeping demands the Trump administration made of Tehran. As Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, said in the early stages of the conflict, “I think both our friends and potential foes are seeing the prowess of the joint force and that also contributes to deterrence.”.

Sources indicate that going back to the early years of the Cold War, the concept of credibility—a state’s perceived capabilities and its willingness to use them even at high cost—has played a central role in the decisions that led to and sustained many of the United States’ largest military campaigns. The need to bolster U.S. credibility was a key force driving Washington’s strategy in Korea and Vietnam in the mid-twentieth century, and it played an notable role in Iraq and Afghanistan during the so-called war on terror. American strategists today continue to assess foreign policy decisions based on how they might strengthen or weaken the country’s reputation.

It has been revealed that but as the results of the Iran campaign have shown, a decision to use force does not always strengthen deterrence. After nearly ten months of war, and the expenditure of billions of dollars of munitions, the United States appears little closer to achieving its objectives of definitively ending Iran’s nuclear threat and ability to project power across the region, let alone securing regime change in Tehran. Meanwhile, the war has badly depleted U.S. military resources that could be used elsewhere and has further eroded the American public’s willingness to support military interventions. Rather than sending a strong signal of U.S. resolve, the Iran war risks conveying the opposite message. Vice President JD Vance argued that the reason the Republicans lost the midterm elections was the Iran war, and government officials in Tehran have gloated that “Americans mentioned no to war.”.

In a recent development, in fact, the conventional wisdom that standing firm in a military conflict enhances a state’s credibility misses something key. As the U.S. wars in Vietnam and Iraq demonstrated, a prolonged military campaign may leave the country more cautious about using force, and less willing to bear the costs, in the years that follow. Adversaries notice this. Given that prior efforts by the Trump administration to compromise with Tehran were criticized as “appeasement” by figures like former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence, Trump may be tempted to continue or even expand the Iran campaign. But by taxing U.S. capabilities and deepening war-weariness among the American public, escalation in Iran could instead lead Beijing and Moscow to question Washington’s appetite for future interventions.

Sources indicate that policymakers should be far more skeptical about using military force for the sake of demonstrating U.S. resolve, and they should be less averse to backing down. The Cold War competition with the Soviet Union convinced the United States to intervene in costly proxy wars that consumed enormous human and military resources for questionable gain, and now the strategic competition with China and Russia may do the same. These kinds of conflicts are precisely the ones that are likely to harm, rather than help, U.S. credibility. Instead of obsessing about its reputation for resolve, which it cannot control, Washington must refocus its attention on maintaining the military strength and capabilities it needs to deter its major adversaries. Sometimes the best way to preserve both the capability and the willingness to act in the future is to walk away from conflict in the present.

In a recent development, for decades, policymakers and scholars have treated a country’s credibility as the dark matter of international politics—a hard-to-measure attribute that is nonetheless enormously crucial for maintaining deterrence. In the 1960s, nuclear deterrence theorist and Nobel Prize winner Thomas Schelling went so far as to say that acquiring a reputation for resolve is “one of the few things worth fighting over.” In keeping with this, it has long been assumed that whereas standing firm communicates to adversaries and allies alike that a country is willing to run risks and bear costs to uphold its interests, backing down or seeking to compromise conveys the opposite. As a result, many U.S. leaders and strategists have drawn on the logic of credibility to justify the most hawkish policies toward adversaries: making maximalist demands, using force, and remaining in wars long past the point where their costs exceeded their benefits.

Vietnam was a case in point. When debating whether to send the first group of U.S. troops to Vietnam in 1965, U.S. Secretary of State Dean Rusk told President Lyndon Johnson, “If the Communist world finds out we will not pursue our commitments to the end, I don’t know where they will stay their hand.” Later, as the United States became bogged down in the war, Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton went further, arguing in a formerly top-secret memo that the primary reason for continuing the Vietnam War was to maintain America’s “reputation as a guarantor” and “avoid a humiliating U.S. defeat.” According to this logic, 58,000 U.S. soldiers and likely over a million Vietnamese people were killed not because the outcome of the war was itself crucial to U.S. interests, but because Washington worried how others—especially the Soviets—would perceive it if it withdrew.

In a recent development, since the Cold War, the same justifications have been used to push the country into, and to sustain, many other conflicts. This was especially true during the so-called Forever Wars the United States was drawn into after the 9/11 attacks. On the night of 9/11, U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld noted, “We need to bomb something else [other than the relatively weak Taliban] to prove that we’re, you know, big and strong and not going to be pushed around by these kinds of attacks.” The logic of credibility not only played a role in Washington launching the Iraq war in 2003 but also locked it into the conflict, even as the costs rose and the raison d’être for the war—weapons of mass destruction—turned out to be false. As President George W. Bush said in 2006, “If we were to leave before the mission is complete, it would hurt U.S. credibility.”.

Industry observers note that conversely, strategists have been quick to criticize U.S. leaders who backed down. During the Syrian civil war, many were concerned about the reputational damage to the United States when President Barack Obama declined to respond to the Syrian government’s use of sarin gas to attack a rebel-held suburb of Damascus, thereby violating a red line that Obama had previously declared. In 2021, many foreign policy hawks reprimanded President Joe Biden for withdrawing from Afghanistan and for waiving some U.S. sanctions on Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline project. At the time, Michael McCaul, the top Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, remarked, “U.S. credibility from Kyiv to Taipei cannot withstand another blow of this nature.” More recently, Trump himself has been accused of backing down against China on tariffs, which some have decried as another example of “Trump always chickens out,” or “TACO.” In each of these cases, critics argued that Washington’s failure to act has compromised the perception that the United States is willing to run risks and bear costs to achieve its objectives.

Despite the persistent assumption that U.S. credibility requires using force and refusing to back down, that thinking has been repeatedly challenged over the past decade. For one thing, experience has shown that a country’s past behavior may be a poor indicator of its present-day resolve. In April, for example, The Latest York Times reported that Trump believed that Iran was unlikely to attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz based on its past actions—such as its failure to mount a robust response to the U.S. and Israeli bombing of its nuclear facilities in the 12-day war in 2025. In reality, however, Iran has been far less restrained than expected in the current conflict and moved quickly not only to close the strait but also to attack U.S. allies and U.S. military bases across the region. In other words, Tehran’s failure to stand firm in 2025 had little bearing on its resolve in the present war.

In any case, it is far from clear that a country’s reputation for resolve is something that it can control by its actions alone. As Keren Yarhi-Milo has explained in Foreign Affairs, “credibility is in the eye of the beholder.” Even if a state acts decisively to signal strength, an adversary may not interpret that action as reason to reconsider its behavior. For example, despite Washington’s intention to communicate high resolve by bearing tremendous costs in the Vietnam War, the North Vietnamese Communist Party Central Committee concluded in 1965 that “the domestic situation in the United States, however, will not allow them to fully utilize their economic and military power in their war of aggression.” In other words, Hanoi ignored the intended signal from Washington and refused to back down.

Sources indicate that other pitfalls are associated with demonstrating resolve by standing firm and fighting. At the extreme, a state that leans too much on military strength can gain a reputation for aggression in ways that undermine long-term deterrence. Napoleonic France and Nazi Germany both had strong reputations for resolve, but their offensive actions ultimately provoked other countries rather than deterring them. There is certainly a risk that U.S. actions under the second Trump administration—such as decapitating the Iranian government and threatening to annex Canada, Gaza, and Greenland—could similarly backfire. For example, there is growing evidence that U.S. allies and partners in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia are rethinking their reliance on the United States and are seeking other sources of security. Far from conceding to Trump’s demands, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described a “rupture” in relations between Washington and Ottawa and advocated for middle powers to band together to protect their sovereignty.

It has been revealed that even if using force bolsters a country’s reputation for resolve, it may harm the country’s broader credibility. For instance, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and its willingness to absorb hundreds of thousands of casualties since then has sent a strong signal about its resolve. Yet its dramatic underperformance on the battlefield against a far smaller and less well-equipped army has likely diminished the international perception of its military effectiveness. The war in Iran could similarly tarnish the United States’ military reputation. Since February, Washington has depleted at least half of its precision-strike missiles and advanced air defense interceptor missiles. It will likely take years to replenish these stockpiles given slow manufacturing times for so-called exquisite platforms. In the meantime, the United States has fewer advanced systems to draw on if China makes a move against Taiwan or if Russia attacks Poland or Estonia. For both Russia’s and the United States’ military campaigns, then, the net effect has been to reduce rather than enhance the countries’ reputation for military capability in the eyes of their respective adversaries.

Quite apart from the negative consequences that often come with decisions to use force, there is an even more fundamental problem with conventional thinking about credibility. In practice, backing down can actually be more helpful to a country’s reputation for resolve than fighting. This becomes especially clear in looking at the long-term effects of engaging in military interventions. Although the United States was victorious in World War I, the conflict produced a lingering war-weariness among the U.S. public and key policymakers. In the years after the Armistice, Americans expressed strong support for the idea that the United States should stay out of any future European war, a sentiment that was ultimately codified in the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s. Only after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, more than two years after war began in Europe, did the United States enter World War II. Fighting in World War I sent a signal of strong resolve to adversaries, but Americans’ war-weariness and resurgent isolationism in the years that followed conveyed that the United States would be less resolved to fight.

This dynamic has been even more apparent in the aftermath of major U.S. wars since then. Following the Vietnam War, President Jimmy Carter declared that “young Americans should never again be sent to die in battle unless our own nation is endangered.” Consider how this kind of thinking affected adversaries’ view of the United States: In deciding to invade Kuwait in 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein assumed that the United States was intensely casualty averse and might not intervene or would back down swiftly. General Wafiq al-Samarrai, Iraq’s head of military intelligence during the Gulf War, said in a 1996 interview that Saddam “thought that America’s involvement in Vietnam had badly damaged its willingness to use military power.” Although the Vietnam War was primarily fought to buttress the United States’ reputation for resolve, it had the opposite effect in practice.

According to recent reports, and again, during and after the U.S. war in Iraq, Americans became skeptical of costly military interventions. As a result, recent administrations have been especially hesitant to commit ground troops in combat operations. Iran is undoubtedly aware of this so-called Iraq syndrome, which may embolden Tehran to act more aggressively without having to fear a large-scale American ground operation.

There is also experimental evidence that backing down may strengthen a country’s long-term reputation for resolve. In a survey I conducted in 2021 with 100 British parliamentarians, respondents were randomly divided into two groups. The first group read about a situation in which a hypothetical country backed down from a prior conflict. The second group read about a hypothetical country that stood firm in a prior conflict but displayed the same signs of war-weariness or “syndromes” that emerged in the United States after the Vietnam and Iraq wars. Both groups were then asked to estimate the likelihood that the country in question would stand firm or back down in a current dispute with the United Kingdom. On average, parliamentarians believed that the country that backed down in the prior dispute would have greater resolve in the current dispute. In other words, if fighting leads to war-weariness, then backing down can actually be better for a state’s future credibility.

It has been revealed that as the U.S. campaign in Iran has demonstrated, choosing to fight to maintain a reputation for resolve is an incredibly risky gamble and may backfire. To avoid repeating the same mistake, U.S. policymakers and strategists need to rethink the relationship between credibility and fighting. First, the United States should avoid fighting altogether when the primary objective is shoring up reputation rather than defending a core national problem. If a conflict directly involves key security and economic interests, as did the U.S. Revolutionary War and World War II, then fighting can be a logical choice, assuming the United States has sufficient military capabilities to win the war at reasonable cost. But if the primary argument for the war relates to future credibility, as in Vietnam, then policymakers should be wary.

Industry observers note that second, if Washington determines that an adversary must be confronted with military force, then it must focus on limited, achievable objectives. Wars that drag on because they have much larger aims, or are prolonged simply for reputational reasons, may erode the country’s credibility by draining munitions and making Americans more reluctant to fight in the future. The two U.S. interventions against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq illustrate this point well. In the limited 1991 Gulf War, the United States swiftly expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait at low cost and before war-weariness could set in among the U.S. public. But the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, in which Washington pursued the far more expansive goal of regime change, continued for years at high cost and made many U.S. policymakers and ordinary citizens alike less supportive of using force in the future.

Finally, policymakers should focus less on the U.S. reputation for resolve, which they cannot control, and more on the country’s military capabilities, which they can. To deter Beijing and Moscow, Washington needs to convince both adversaries that it has the ability to prosecute a modern great-power war. The problem is that, although the United States continues to have the most advanced military capabilities and weapons systems in the world, they are limited in quantity, extremely expensive, and take a long time to replace. In the course of just a few months of fighting against Iran, the United States depleted huge percentages of its advanced and expensive stockpiles of offensive and defensive missiles.

Recent findings suggest that this alarming shortfall raises newly introduced questions about whether the United States could sustain a longer war of attrition of the type Russia and Ukraine are fighting. Washington urgently needs to replenish its stockpiles and rethink its dependence on a small number of exquisite systems. It also needs to avoid costly conflicts that distract it from the principal threats it faces from China and Russia. Rather than making U.S. credibility stronger in the eyes of the world, continuing the war in Iran could well undermine it, just as fighting in Vietnam and Iraq did.

Why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

According to recent reports, these are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the upcoming memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

According to recent reports, why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir, Bob Woodward, Simon & Schuster, 592 pp., $35, November 2026.

These are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the new memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

It has been revealed that woodward, of course, became famous as one half of the reporting duo that broke open the Watergate story (the other being Carl Bernstein), prompting the 1974 resignation of President Richard Nixon. Since then, he’s produced books on everything from the Supreme Court (The Brethren) to the doomed comedian John Belushi. But starting with his 1991 book, The Commanders, Woodward has spent a good part of his later career exploring what he calls “the most serious action a president can take”: declaring war.

Much has been written about President Donald Trump’s ill-justified war against Iran that began earlier this year, and whether his controversial defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, should bear the blame for giving Trump far-too-optimistic assurances of success. But this bumbling process, such as it was, has ample precedent going back to the Vietnam War. Time after time, presidents have botched it badly, Woodward writes, for almost always for the same reasons: a failure to thoroughly hash out the pitfalls before they pull the trigger, and a commensurate failure by their senior staff to deliver tough, honest assessments of the risks.

With a couple of exceptions, such as Brent Scowcroft, President George H.W. Bush’s national security advisor, or Colin Powell, George W. Bush’s first secretary of state, presidents rarely get the straight story from their advisors, Woodward writes.

According to recent reports, “I have seen clearly over a half century of reporting on 11 presidents how crucial it is that a president understand that part of their job is to find ways to puncture the treacherous curtain of deference around them,” he writes. “Others might call it Oval Office Freeze, not wanting to bring bad news to a president or framing something in a way that panders to their ego or worldview.”.

In a recent development, this deep dysfunction, Woodward suggests, is the throughline from Lyndon Johnson in Vietnam, who was ill-served by his defense secretary, Robert McNamara, and other senior military officials; to George W. Bush, who was fraudulently persuaded to invade Iraq by Vice President Dick Cheney, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, and CIA Director George Tenet.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson and Defense Secretary Robert McNamara react during a meeting at the White House in Washington on Feb. 7, 1968. Yoichi Okamoto/Johnson White House Photographs/NARA/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that trump’s ill-advised aggression against Iran—which has degenerated into a draining, nine-month conflict with no end in sight—is only the latest example of governmental ineptitude at the highest level, resulting in the unnecessary loss of innocent lives and a decline in U.S. prestige and power. Trump introduced “a destructive and bloody war with no legal authority,” Woodward writes. “His impulsive decision to start a war with Iran is the clearest example of what happens when there is no one to say, ‘Wait a minute, what are the consequences?’”.

Sources indicate that what’s most unnerving, perhaps, is that this ego-driven impulse to launch unnecessary wars may have grown more haphazard at a time when war has grown more dangerous. AI-driven autonomous systems are increasingly coming to dominate command and control, and presidential decisions to respond to threats sometimes must be made in minutes or seconds. Under recent concepts like the Defense Department’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control—which connects all branches of the armed forces into a unified, AI-powered network—conventional and nuclear war strategy is being combined in newly introduced ways, experts say. And in an era when many missiles are “dual use,” strategists may not know if an incoming missile has a conventional or a nuclear warhead.

Beijing appears to be implementing similar systems, and despite the historic trilateral summit this week between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, there are almost no negotiated restraints in place between the United States, China, and Russia.

It has been revealed that woodward writes that the threat of accidental nuclear war has haunted him since his earliest days. Just out of Yale on an ROTC scholarship in the mid-1960s, he served on a Navy communications ship designed as a relocation site for the president in the event of a national security emergency, especially nuclear war. Swiftly he realized how easily the locks on the nuclear codes could be broken.

“I felt a little ill at the absurdity of it all—to have weapons of such destructive potential and to give me, a 22-year-old ensign, responsibility related to their use,” he writes. “My mind worried endlessly over the possible scenarios that could cause the nuclear procedures and safeguards to break down. What were the fatal flaws? There seemed to be far too many.”.

Industry observers note that later on, as a renowned reporter interviewing high-level U.S. officials, including McNamara and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, Woodward says he came to realize how disturbingly real his early fears were. “Nuclear procedures were still a mess,” he writes. Woodward quotes McNamara—the erstwhile hawk who in retirement became an advocate for the abolition of nuclear weapons—as saying, “You could never control a nuclear war.”.

Sources indicate that today at age 83, Woodward says he’s still scared—perhaps more so. “At heart, I am still the shaken 22-year-old junior Navy officer who witnessed the weak locks on the safes guarding authentication codes for using US nuclear weapons and imagined how easily it could all go wrong,” Woodward writes. “I have always been a catastrophic thinker, but these days the dangers feel more present and grave.”.

In a recent development, from right: U.S. President George W. Bush meets with Vice President Dick Cheney and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld outside the White House Oval Office in Washington on March 19, 2003, shortly after authorizing Operation Iraqi Freedom. Eric Draper/White House/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that this theme of self-defeating war begins to emerge in Woodward’s book through an extraordinary series of interviews Woodward had with McNamara before the latter died in 2009. In excruciating detail, the anguished McNamara explains to Woodward why, during Vietnam, he failed utterly to insist on a “knock-down, drag-out debate over the loose assumptions, unasked questions and thin analyses underlying our military strategy.” McNamara astonishes Woodward by telling the reporter that not only was the U.S. military not “open in discussing their views with either the president or me,” McNamara himself didn’t really question the military at all.

“I don’t think the books today reviewing the Vietnam War give adequate attention to the failure of the senior military leaders to acquaint their civilian counterparts with their feelings that we were on a hopeless course” in Vietnam, McNamara mentioned.

Woodward’s response? “I was aghast,” he writes.

Recent findings suggest that but no fixes were ever put in place. On the contrary, as time went on, the decision-making process became even less systematic. Earlier this year, critics blasted Trump officials for saying he was attacking Iran because, as then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt said, “The president had a feeling … that Iran was going to strike the United States.” In fact, there was no evidence of a planned Iranian attack.

Warnings about transnational radicalism are rooted in the same accusations that sought to silence a renowned reporter decades ago.

The famous thinker’s latest memoir reveals a fateful political and intellectual blind spot.

It’s the strategic disaster that keeps on giving.

But how different was Trump’s “feeling” from Bush saying the decision to launch a preventive war against Iraq came from his “gut”? It isn’t, Woodward suggests.

It has been revealed that “In hindsight it is evident that not enough people got in Bush’s way. No one said, let’s slow down. What are we really trying to achieve here?” Woodward writes. As Bush told Woodward in an interview: “I’m not a textbook player, I’m a gut player.” Translation: The war in Iraq had no basis in careful analysis whatsoever.

Just as there is no record of Trump debating the wisdom of a newly introduced war against Iran with his national security team, McNamara concedes the same was largely true of Vietnam.

“The [Joint Chiefs of Staff] never really discussed the military blueprint for Vietnam,” he told Woodward. “I don’t think you’ll find any record, secret or otherwise, of the chiefs’ critical analysis of the military plans in Vietnam.” As McNamara later admits, the Vietnam War had nothing to do with the superpower conflict between the United States and Soviet Union or the “domino theory” of the Cold War but was, instead “a civil war, not an external war.” It was, as Woodward writes, “In effect a no-win policy.”.

Industry observers note that mcNamara points to a map of Vietnam during a news conference in Washington on April 26, 1965. Marion S Trikosko/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

Similarly, when it came to examining the premises of the Iraq invasion, “McNamara’s lesson was once again ignored.” There is no record that the Bush team ever held a serious debate about the wisdom of going into Iraq.

“I could not help but think of Vietnam,” Woodward writes about the Iraq invasion. Bush, pressed repeatedly by Woodward, reveals in a series of interviews not long after the war began in 2003 that he had no real justification for his world-altering decision to attack Iraq other than the idea that Saddam, “given his nature,” might have pursued weapons of mass destruction.

“I look back on this now more than 20 years later and realize his answer was preposterous,” Woodward writes. “I should have pressed him more on this. A leader’s ‘nature’ was not sufficient grounds for invading a country.”.

It has been revealed that nor was there even any longer much “anguish” over the possibility of making a wrong decision, as there was during Vietnam. Woodward writes that he told McNamara in one of their interviews that he tried to find evidence of “anguished memos” about Iraq similar to the ones McNamara had secretly written about Vietnam in 1967.

It has been revealed that the Bush team’s response? “‘There’s no anguish,’ they said. ‘Well, that’s what’s wrong with them,’ McNamara declared. ‘I’ll tell you, because there ought to be anguish.’” Woodward writes: “I did not respond but I agreed fully—more anguish might have stopped the war.”.

Sources indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump, flanked by CIA Director John Ratcliffe (left), Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (right), and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine (far right), addresses a news conference at the White House on April 6.Andrew Harnik/Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that in his typical fashion, as he’s done through most of the 24 books he’s produced, Woodward plays the pure reporter who does little historical analysis and rarely passes judgment. Though in his last book, War, he called Trump  “the most reckless and impulsive president in history,” he doesn’t repeat that assessment here. Indeed, Woodward relates most of these conversations without giving any real historical context at all.

Industry observers note that nor does Woodward allow himself much, if any, psychological analysis of the historic figures he’s spent so many hours with. For example, he reports on his conversations with Joe Biden, in which the then-vice president says the military was overselling President Barack Obama on the war in Afghanistan and boasts, “The military doesn’t fuck around with me.”.

But it seems clear that it was Biden’s overconfidence in his own judgment that led him, as president, to ignore accurate assessments from his own military advisors about the rapid collapse of the Afghan government and subsequent takeover by the Taliban in 2021.

Sources indicate that still, Woodward does tend toward some broad conclusions. He quotes the late historian David McCullough as saying that the greatest acts of presidents involve not going to war.

“The examples he gave me all shared one element: restraint. The most notable decision John Adams made was not to go to war with France, McCullough told me.” Similarly, Dwight Eisenhower’s “greatest series of decisions was keeping United States troops out of Vietnam.”.

U.S. President John F. Kennedy meets with military leaders in the Oval Office on Oct. 16, 1962, to discuss surveillance of Cuba. Charles Phelps Cushing/ClassicStock/Getty Images.

According to recent reports, again quoting McNamara, Woodward also notes that John F. Kennedy, unusually for a president, defied the majority of his national security team when they voted in favor of attacking Cuba during the 1962 Cuban missile crisis—voting, in effect, to go to war with the USSR. “The vote is 9 to 8 in favor of attacking and destroying the missiles, Kennedy announced to the group, and without pausing stated as clear as a bell, ‘The eights have it,’” Woodward quotes McNamara as saying.

He concludes: “Looking back, the world was safer because President Kennedy believed his primary responsibility as commander in chief of the most powerful military in the world was to avoid war where possible.”.

According to recent reports, michael Hirsh is a columnist for Foreign Policy. #99592. The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2545 w)

The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026.
  • Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.
  • According to recent reports, as the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

According to recent reports, as the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

Sources indicate that but one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is important in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

Sources indicate that as the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an important precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

Industry observers note that today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many issues. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

Industry observers note that the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

Sources indicate that yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

According to recent reports, these tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

That began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a new and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more vital.

In practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience revealed that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up upcoming horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian issue. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

But these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more important. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

In recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

Recent findings suggest that but there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

In a recent development, I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafes and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

The result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

Sources indicate that the debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place reveals how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

Industry observers note that in the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Industry observers note that beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental problems of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

According to recent reports, I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

Industry observers note that thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

Industry observers note that there is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fox News' Madeline Rivera provides details on a reported cyberattack after a string of outages with the FBI at the center of this attack. Rivera says this is the second breach in recent months.

Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.

The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but, for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources said.

The NCIC database is a critical information-sharing tool for federal, state and local authorities, helping them track fugitives, monitor registered sex offenders, check whether someone has failed a gun background check, among other information.

In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Saturday morning, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack.

The FBI headquarters building in Washington D.C., Feb. 20, 2026. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images).

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS.

"I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that," Trump added.

Industry observers note that the FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNN first reported the hack.

In September, a group called ShinyHunters hacked into the FBI's job portal website intending to steal sensitive employment records.

The mysterious group, known for extortion plots, claimed it stole sensitive information belonging to almost every FBI agent, including names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, the names of family members.

It has been revealed that FBI agents walk down Florida Avenue, between 14th Street NW and 13th Strreet NW, Aug. 13, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images).

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER.

The details of Dubrovsky's alleged crimes are unknown because the court records in relation to his case remain sealed.

FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed the arrest of ShinyHunters "suspected co-conspirator" on Oct. 9, a day after Dubrovsky was taken into custody.

  • Sources indicate that video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the biggest single media event of the decade took place on Thursday, and most of Washington missed it. Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment of the most popular video game series in the world, racked up nearly $1.5 billion in sales even before it launched, already making back what may have been a more-than-a-billion dollar budget. In the next week, total sales are projected to hit over $3 billion. The previous game in the series still makes half a billion dollars a year through its online version alone. (For comparison purposes, Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, the biggest concert tour of all time, took in just over $2 billion, while Avengers: Endgame grossed roughly $2.9 billion.).

Sources indicate that video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. As industry consultant George Osborn points out in his new book, Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, video gaming, once a solitary activity, has become a largely communal one. Online play creates a “third place” where people, especially the young, can mingle. As Osborn puts it, “what happens in video games communities bleeds out into reality—all the way into our political discourse.”.

Industry observers note that the biggest single media event of the decade took place on Thursday, and most of Washington missed it. Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment of the most popular video game series in the world, racked up nearly $1.5 billion in sales even before it launched, already making back what may have been a more-than-a-billion dollar budget. In the next week, total sales are projected to hit over $3 billion. The previous game in the series still makes half a billion dollars a year through its online version alone. (For comparison purposes, Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, the biggest concert tour of all time, took in just over $2 billion, while Avengers: Endgame grossed roughly $2.9 billion.).

According to recent reports, power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, George E. Osborn, Prometheus, 376 pp., July 2026, $34.95.

Recent findings suggest that video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. As industry consultant George Osborn points out in his latest book, Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, video gaming, once a solitary activity, has become a largely communal one. Online play creates a “third place” where people, especially the young, can mingle. As Osborn puts it, “what happens in video games communities bleeds out into reality—all the way into our political discourse.”.

Under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for instance, Saudi Arabia has become a major force in video games, mostly through the power of capital. The prince, himself a keen gamer, is trying to encourage the creation of a domestic industry. He’s had little success so far, but Saudi money has succeeded in buying up existing companies, such as the giant Electronic Arts for $55 billion and the tech giant that created Pokémon Go for $3.5 billion.

Sources indicate that mohammed bin Salman wants to make money. But, as Osborn points out, he also wants to get gullible or greedy Westerners to help whitewash his corrupt, misogynistic autocracy. Buying gaming companies may be a more expensive route than donating to D.C. think tanks, but also perhaps a more effective one. Some industry insiders have already flagged worries about Saudi censorship in their games.

Recent findings suggest that an artist rendering of “The Line” in an undated image. NEOM.

In a recent development, but if the Saudi government is shaping video games, the influence is going the other way as well. Consider some of the crown prince’s grandiose projects. His plan for The Line, a 106-mile-long and 650-foot-wide city, appeared to be inspired by the futuristic cities that appear in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Deus Ex. The difference, of course, was that in reality The Line project was suspended after only 1.5 miles of foundation were dug.

That feedback loop between gaming and reality is also evident when looking at another of Osborn’s case studies, Russia. Especially since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian studios have churned out propaganda games such as Squad 22: ZOV, which Osborn describes as an “objectively bad video game” but also a hub for anti-Ukrainian memes and a gathering place for ultranationalists.

Recent findings suggest that the fantasies of Russian games hook back into wider influence efforts. With the help of influencers such as streamer GrishaPutin, these games aim to boost morale and recruitment while also luring in foreign fighters, roughly 11,000 of whom have died fighting on the Russian side. Australian Daryl Fladung has been missing, believed dead, for several months after being recruited to come and fight for Russia (and post propaganda videos) through online war games. His last videos show him terrified and in pain.

Recent findings suggest that australian Daryl Fladung (right) and two fellow Russia-supporting British nationals on arrival in Moscow in an undated photo. Telegram: Ben Stimson.

According to recent reports, russia’s reactionary politics are also attractive to some gamers. The gender split in gaming is roughly equal nowadays but the third place of popular games has a habit of becoming dominated by the loudest young men. It’s not uncommon for female players to conceal their gender, or even use a voice changer, to avoid harassment.

According to recent reports, that too has bled back into politics. Video game writers are generally liberal progressives, and there was a substantial push toward broadening representation in games in the 2010s, with female protagonists and people of color becoming more normalized. This was welcomed by many gamers but prompted a reactionary fury from others. The movement that resulted was Gamergate, which became part of the far-right’s attempt to woo younger male voters, with the encouragement of Steve Bannon. While it may have helped tip elections toward Donald Trump, it failed to produce any good games of its own.

Despite being the biggest video game market in the world, compared to Moscow, Beijing is far more reluctant to throw its weight around in gaming propaganda overseas. That’s in part because of a puritan communist dislike of any form of fun, leading to repeated crackdowns on minors playing games online and long delays before latest games are officially approved.

Recent findings suggest that censorship at home is massive but, as Osborn notes, “Chinese games businesses invested billions of dollars in games businesses across the world to soften the blows landing on them from the CCP.” (pg. 151). Apart from some policing around Hong Kong and Taiwanese representation in games, those investments have mostly remained business-focused rather than trying to impose political limits. As with much else, China’s focus has been domestic control first, and foreign influence second.

It has been revealed that the Honor of Kings International Championship in Shenzhen, China, on Dec. 3, 2022. Honor of Kings, a multiplayer online battle arena game, is operated by Tencent, China’s largest video game publisher.Honor of Kings/Tencent.

But perhaps gaming’s biggest global influence lies in its role driving the AI industry, a story Osborn doesn’t cover in depth because much of it is so recent. Gaming depends on video cards, which are built with the high-end chips that also fuel the AI revolution. In fiscal year 2018, for instance, Nvidia made roughly 57 percent of its income from gaming. Last year, that figure was 7 percent, with roughly 90 percent coming from AI data centers.

Recent findings suggest that osborn highlights the role gaming played in driving forward the innovation needed for newer and better technology, especially in chip design. But the shift of the industry toward AI has left gamers deeply angry at Nvidia, a manufacturer they once adored. (As a result, some of the best investigative reporting on Jensen Huang’s fall and Nvidia’s role in evading U.S. sanctions on China has come out of the games media.) Gaming hardware used to be getting cheaper and cheaper; the same setup would be half the price two years later. Thanks to the AI race, the reverse is now true. The gaming PC I bought for $1,600 the week Trump was elected for a second time, anticipating tariff rises, now retails at $2,600. It might seem a little silly to care deeply about your toys getting more expensive. But the contestation between gamers and AI companies is a microcosm of a wider glitch: Who controls technological power?

Recent findings suggest that screen captures of the survival horror game Resident Evil Requiem, released in February, showing Nvidia’s latest graphics rendering model DLSS 5. It uses AI to infuse pixels with photorealistic lighting and materials. NVIDIA.

Personal computers have been the domain of tinkerers and inventors since they were first introduced at home. Now Sam Altman has put forward, then rapidly retracted, the idea that having RAM sitting in your own PC is “terrible” because it should be used by mega-corporations instead. In this context, the growing revolt against AI in video games—with players boycotting games that use AI art, AI writing, or even AI code—feels like part of something bigger.

Osborn’s final chapters are dedicated to promoting games that educate citizens and support the fight for democracy worldwide, from pro-Ukrainian stories to “green game jams” to promote climate awareness. But as long as the industry, and the technology that powers it, is in the hands of autocrats and tech tycoons, these aren’t the games we’ll be playing.
